This study investigates the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks for calculating the largest eigenvalue of the Schrödinger operator in high-dimensional settings. It demonstrates that a specific method involving a Gaussian activation function achieves a certain level of error reduction in the largest eigenvalue of the Schrödinger operator under certain conditions. Furthermore, a related neural network is developed to solve the eigenvalue problem for the Laplace operator with inhomogeneous additions, and the research shows that the algorithm performs well even in the limit of very high dimensions. The findings highlight the potential of using neural networks to solve critical problems in physics. An open-source code implementation of the findings is available under the MIT License at the following repository: https://github.com/alutig/phys2layer. In evaluating the likelihood of outcome for breast cancer patients, determining the quantity of lymphatic cells that have crossed the basement membrane is crucial. Yet, this process is extremely time-consuming for pathologists to perform. A deep learning approach can simplify this process, and to test this, a virtual microenvironment dataset was created. Based on this, a training method using only the existing cancer patients' data, and without acquiring new data, was developed to facilitate quantification. This training method uses federated learning to overcome hardware limitations and is demonstrated to be effective in multiple TIL categorization tasks. When applied to real clinical data, the entire model's performance can be assessed, and as a result, a more accurate prediction of patient outcomes and treatment decisions can be made. This research enables the widespread adoption of deep learning in routine clinical settings, and as such, may offer new possibilities for understanding and treating cancer. A versatile approach to teaching robots to walk is reinforcement learning, but it demands a detailed reward function that specifies the goal and desired behavior. In many situations, defining such a function is challenging due to the complexity of the task. We present a new, collaborative method that combines reinforcement learning with an evolutionary algorithm to generate suitable training pathways. Unlike prior approaches that rely on pre-defined trajectories or social learning, our evolved pathway generator creates multiple dynamic training pathways adaptively through an evolutionary process. As a result, robots can learn control policies that move efficiently along these generated pathways, focused on the most important learning steps. The effectiveness of this method was tested on a quadrupedal robot and demonstrated to yield better navigation and learning performance than traditional reinforcement learning and other state-of-the-art approaches. Additionally, this method yielded improved generalization of learning outcomes, as well as a more stable and predictable training process. The nature of hot active galactic nuclei (AGN) winds, particularly those in low-luminosity AGN, remains unclear. This is because the issue of whether AGN winds are radiative or wind-driven by a central supermassive black hole has not been fully addressed by existing observations. We present new high-resolution X-ray spectra of the low-luminosity AGN in the NGC 7213 galaxy, which reveals the presence of Fe XXVI and Fe XXV absorption lines indicative of warm and hot outflows. This observation of metal-rich outflows from low-luminosity AGN, which cannot be explained by stellar processes, provides evidence for an alternative scenario where AGN winds are initiated by a central feedback mechanism. Additionally, the properties of the hot outflow in NGC 7213 are similar to those of a "hot breeze" that has been predicted to exist in theories of black hole feedback. This discovery of a hot breeze in NGC 7213, rather than a high-velocity wind, may imply that black hole feedback could be inefficient at launching high-velocity winds, but rather contributes to a more slowly moving, gas-rich atmosphere that can facilitate black hole feedback through interaction with surrounding interstellar medium. This a hot breeze could be the primary agent of black hole feedback, which is necessary for resolving the galactic feedback paradox. Future observations of the NGC 7213 galaxy at other wavelengths will be necessary to confirm the presence of this hot breeze. This research explores a system management challenge, specifically focusing on controlling a specific type of rotor flow using the nonlinear optimal regulator (NOR) model-reference control method. However, implementing NOR requires extensive knowledge of sensor and actuator dynamics, which can be highly complicated and infeasible. To address this limitation, we turn to model-free control approaches that don't require this detailed dynamics information. Although model-free strategies often lack performance compared to their traditional counterparts, advanced reinforcement learning techniques have shown potential in improving model-free control performance. Specifically, we investigate the potential of two-phase reinforcement learning (2ph-RL) as a model-free approach that learns actuator-sensor policies without relying on detailed system models. Our 2ph-RL approach leverages the model predictive control (MPC) framework, combining the strengths of model-free and model-based strategies within a unified framework. Our simulation results indicate that 2ph-RL can not only enable stable model-free control but also facilitate the convergence of associated MPC schemes. Furthermore, 2ph-RL's performance compares favorably to state-of-the-art model-free and reinforcement learning-based strategies, particularly in scenarios with limited and unlimited actuator availability. To validate 2ph-RL's effectiveness in real-world applications, we apply it to the reconfiguration of a nonlinear jet engine model-reference control system, obtaining the desired evidence. Our 2ph-RL approach is poised to empower researchers with a novel model-free and reinforcement learning-based methodology for tackling various system management challenges. Additionally, its potential to replace traditional model-based strategies in real-time processing systems makes 2ph-RL an essential tool for controlling complex industrial systems. Our 2ph-RL software toolkit, complete with demonstration codes, is openly accessible online at https://github.com/AE-ML/2ph-RL-toolkit. Our study addresses a critical shortcoming in current reinforcement learning research by examining the practical feasibility and performance of model-free control strategies. Our 2ph-RL approach, characterized by two distinct learning phases and a unique MPC framework, enables smooth transition between model-free and model-based policies, thereby ensuring stable system operation. Our theoretical and practical findings, backed by comprehensive numerical and real-time experimental validation, showcase the efficacy of 2ph-RL in various system management challenges. Our model-free 2ph-RL controller excels over state-of-the-art reinforcement learning-based strategies in terms of stable system operation and fast convergence. Our 2ph-RL approach, capable of handling various system management challenges, is now ready for deployment

The reformed SiD Sensor still incorporates a tungsten-scintillating-fiber tracker but replaces the original silicon detectors with monolithic CMOS silicon-carbon detectors. It also integrates a cryogenic monolithic CMOS device providing precision tracking and global alignment, alongside a scintillating detector for particle identification. The revised design features a trigger system that utilizes particle detection data within the Sensor itself, eliminating the need for an external trigger system. This has resulted in a reduced trigger system's task to select among already relevant events, thereby significantly decreasing costs and complexity. The revised SiD Sensor concept addresses concerns regarding silicon detector durability and technological advancements since its initial proposal. It leverages recent developments in monolithic CMOS technology and tungsten-target detectors to enhance the particle identification detection's sensitivity, particularly for hadron identification and its trigger capability. The increasing number of Earth observation satellites leads to a daily stream of more than 30,000 images, offering invaluable insights into environmental changes, natural disasters, agricultural conditions, and urban development, among many other applications. To effectively analyze this vast satellite imagery, machine learning-based platforms are necessary, enabling rapid and accurate categorization, segmentation, and object detection of complex scenarios, such as monitoring construction site violations or identifying fallen trees in urban areas. Our solution, EarthNets, is an open-source, cloud-based platform that leverages AI and provides a comprehensive workflow for users to upload images, train and deploy models, and access analysis results. With a user-friendly interface and a robust back-end architecture, EarthNets enables easy integration with satellite imagery providers and AI frameworks, making it accessible to users without deep technical knowledge of machine learning. By providing a scalable and secure environment for AI model management, EarthNets allows users to upload and execute models, share results, and track execution history. Our demonstration will showcase a real-world use case of EarthNets in enabling AI-driven analysis of satellite images for environmental monitoring. Additionally, we will discuss the technical aspects and limitations of the platform and highlight its potential applications and future developments. Strategies for addressing these challenges and scaling the platform for widespread adoption are also presented. Our solution and associated tools are available for public download on our website. Identifying anomalies in time series data is a critical concern in multiple fields. Current methods for detecting anomalies typically rely on the use of moving averages or dynamic linear models, which segment the data equally and treat each segment equally, ignoring variations in volatility and ignoring the potential effects of past events on future performance. These methods also fail to provide users with clear and understandable results. Furthermore, the selection of parameters in these methods is often subjective and largely reliant on trial and error. To address these limitations, we introduce a new method called ReAD that specializes in detecting anomalies at a local level. This approach involves using a dynamic window to split the data based on in-sample volatility and then modeling each segment using an ARX method that takes into account both lagged values and external factors. By doing so, ReAD treats each segment equally while considering the influences of past events and treats the last segment specially to avoid predicting the present. Additionally, ReAD uses a quadratic loss function and a Bayesian information criterion (BIC) filter to evaluate and compare the performance of anomalies across segments, providing clear and understandable results. Finally, the selection of parameters in ReAD is automated through a study based on the performance of past metrics, known as feature selection, that aims to identify the most effective parameters for detecting anomalies. The relationship between a galaxy's mass in stars and its surrounding dark matter halo mass remains a persistent question in studying galaxy evolution. By analyzing 106 galaxies from the ATLAS$^{\rm 3D}$ project, our research explores how the mass in stars and dark matter changes over time for different galaxy types. Interestingly, our findings reveal a notable difference in mass conversion efficiency among elliptical galaxies compared to spiral and disk galaxies. Specifically, elliptical galaxies are more efficient at converting mass into stars, particularly at higher mass ranges, whereas spiral and disk galaxies exhibit more efficient mass conversion in the lower mass ranges. This distinction holds significant implications for understanding galaxy evolution and its connection to the mass in dark matter, particularly in the massive end of the galaxy spectrum. The mass in dark matter appears to play a crucial role in regulating the star formation activity in galaxies, and this role may become even more vital as the galaxy's mass in dark matter increases. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that the mass in dark matter plays a pivotal role in shaping galaxy evolution, and this understanding can contribute significantly to theoretical models of galaxy formation. We generated theoretical spectra for the gas within the TW Hydrae system that is relevant to cm-radio waves, considering two scenarios: one in which the disk is being slowly destroyed by photoevaporation and another by magnetic forces that drive gas away from the disk. We compared these predictions with the actual observations of TW Hydrae and found that neither scenario alone perfectly matches the data but a combination of the two does. We identified that the model which includes photoevaporation produces too much emission at higher altitudes above the disk than what is actually observed, while the magnetohydrodynamic model that involves a "disk breeze" that rises into the atmosphere may not adequately account for the small-scale structures and the overall intensity of the emission at larger distances from the disk (especially 5-20 AU). We found that incorporating a turbulent mixing process into the model can explain some but not all of the discrepancies between the predicted and actual emissions. Ultimately, we found that the model which includes photoevaporation may be too aggressive in its treatment of disk destruction, while the MHD model may not adequately take into account the effects of local energy gains and losses in the atmosphere. To advance the development of tone-sandhi algorithms, this paper proposes an innovative method for identifying Chinese tones without requiring a predefined tone model. Our approach categorizes speech segments into voiced or unvoiced areas using an unsupervised algorithm, and then follows the dynamics of the voice, working much like a tracker. By combining this with the forward-backward Kalman filter, we can accurately model and predict Chinese pitch contours. The results of our experiments demonstrate that this method is effective in detecting speech regions and tracking pitch contours at a tolerance of 10 cents. The code for this method has been made available on GitHub. Evaluations demonstrate that our algorithm achieves classification errors of 11.44% for voice, 15.68% for unvoice, and 16.39% for tone, representing a significant improvement over the 18.95% error rate for the baseline unsupervised voicing detector. The performance of our algorithm is comparable to that of recurrent neural networks, and it outperforms it particularly in terms of stability, specifically by a factor of 3.27 for voice, 2.10 for unvoice, and 2.45 for tone. The main advantage of our algorithm is its ability to accurately follow the dynamic changes in pitch contours while maintaining a low tone error rate of 16.39%. Furthermore, the parameter associated with the Kalman filter's forward prediction has a steady state of 0.989, indicating a high level of confidence in the predictions made by the filter. The calculated signal-to-noise ratios for the predictions of our algorithm are 10.73 for the training set and 9.68 for the test set. The method's reliance solely on Chinese speech data for training indicates that it is native-bias-free, thereby addressing concerns about the influence of the trainer's bias. Notably, the algorithm was able to correctly identify Chinese tones in a tone-marked corpus with an error rate of 16.39%, and in a tone-unmarked corpus with an error rate of 19.68%. In this study, we examine the fusion of spatial and frequency attributes within millimeter wave wireless local area networks, specifically focusing on the fusion of beamforming and frequency hopping. Beamforming addresses the challenges of channel side information and multi-cell interference through nulling, whereas frequency hopping mitigates against both flat and correlated interference. To assess the combined impact of these techniques, we analyze the outcome of beamforming and frequency hopping in terms of both spatial and temporal interference. This analysis ultimately enables us to establish a link between system performance and parameters such as SNR, channel condition number, and frequency spacing. Consequently, we propose a hybrid approach for incorporating both beamforming and frequency hopping modes in order to achieve optimal results. Notably, this hybrid mode exhibits a direct connection with the maximum scale of frequency spacing, thereby allowing for real-time adjustment according to given standards. Through numerical simulations, we evaluate the performance of the proposed hybrid approach and compare it with various benchmark techniques. The outcomes of these experiments demonstrate a substantial improvement in outcomes when the proposed hybrid approach is utilized. Specifically, it enables support for up to 18 groups of users in 28 GHz bandwidth, thereby outperforming benchmark techniques in this context. Ultimately, we anticipate that the proposed hybrid approach will serve as a versatile solution for incorporating beamforming and frequency hopping in practical mmWave wireless local area networks. This paper introduces and analyzes new metrics for measuring the behavior of vector-valued random variables in high-dimensional spaces. Our research focuses on a subset of these metrics known as \text{HSY}-(1+\alpha)-norms, which are capable of capturing the dependence structure of certain high-dimensional random variables, as proven in the manuscript. To establish the utility of these metrics, we incorporate them into the construction of empirical priors for linear regression models with unknown error variance under sparsity constraints. Subsequent analysis demonstrates the consistency of resulting Bayesian estimators in both the traditional and weighted least squares contexts. Specifically, our findings reveal that minimizing the \text{HSY}-(1+\alpha)-norm leads to consistent estimates of coefficient vectors in both models. Building upon this framework, we extend our methods to accommodate convex and non-convex constraints, offering a versatile approach for incorporating additional statistical information into the priors. Our methodological innovations are substantiated through simulations and real-world data analysis. Additionally, the theoretical results of this research favor the use of our empirical priors over traditional approaches established in the literature. All source codes associated with this research are available at https://github.com/zhkcsu/emp_pri. Utilizing QCD sum rules and $\eta$-$\eta'$ blending, we successfully identify the correct ground state wave functions and masses for the $\eta$ and $\eta'$ mesons. The process of blending accounts for the interactions between these mesons and their mixing partner, the $\eta'$. The calculated masses, 957.78 MeV and 1835.13 MeV, for the $\eta$ and $\eta'$ respectively, align with current particle physics data. The determined wave functions enable a detailed study of the internal structures of the $\eta$ and $\eta'$ mesons. The results obtained from the first radial correction in the sum rules further validate the identified wave functions. The research also updates the $\eta$-$\eta'$ mixing angle to 34.9 degrees. The study's findings demonstrate that combining QCD sum rules with blending provides a precise method to analyze the internal structures of hadrons and can lead to accurate predictions for light hadronic systems. The research also highlights blending's potential in identifying the wave functions and masses of other particles, such as the $a_0$ and f1(1420) mesons. Beyond the classical behavior of paired spin and orbital angular momenta of $1\hbar$, higher-order associations of angular momentum $l\hbar$ with $l>1$ have been observed. The energy spectrum of these states, known as charge density waves (CDWs), is characterized by a finite set of states for each association. The number of CDWs increases with each increment of the association angular momentum, satisfying a divisibility criterion based on the electron interaction strength. This work provides a general framework for the electron interaction's divisibility in two dimensions. The findings of this study are consistent with experimental observations of CDWs in experiments involving moire superlattices in transition metal dichalcogenides and trigeneide compounds. The observed set of states in these experiments matches the predicted set of states for spin-vortex associations with angular momenta of $2\hbar$ and $3\hbar$. The correspondence between theoretical predictions and experimental findings in two different materials validates the theoretical model and identifies the origin of the observed phenomena as spin-vortex associations with higher-order angular momentum. The existence of spin-vortex associations with angular momenta of $l\hbar$ with $l>1$ also provides a possible explanation for the previously unexplained phenomena of polarization-dependent photoluminescence in these materials. The observed polarization-dependent photoluminescence can be attributed to the presence of CDWs associated with angular momenta of $2\hbar$ and $3\hbar$. The proposed model offers a unifying scenario to explain various observed phenomena in these materials as different CDWs. The study establishes a new field of study - electron associations with higher-order angular momenta - and provides a new model for understanding electron behavior in two-dimensional gases with interactions. Privately sharing curated content with specific individuals has become increasingly important, but current graph privacy models fail to address this need as they rely on an external authority determining the sharing scope. This leads to over-restrictive policies that would reveal sensitive information, such as a person's close relationships. To address this gap, this research focuses on developing a new framework that incorporates user-controlled selection of sharing content and corresponding neighbors. An implementation of this concept, called Content-driven Graph Privacy, is presented as a modular approach comprising multiple methods for content and neighbor selection, as well as an adaptable metric to gauge post-disclosure impact. An instance of this framework, specifically designed for academic network research, is also demonstrated. Our approach outperforms existing models in maintaining privacy while preserving network insights, as evidenced by comprehensive experiments. For example, when applying CDGP to the Facebook100 dataset, our method shows significant improvements over traditional models by reducing the disclosure of 8.64% more edge instances and 11.83% more node instances in the worst-case scenario while preserving 96.42% of the network's nodes. The corresponding source code is available at https://github.com/jbarridoj/CDGP. This research introduces a novel method for private content sharing on graphs, addressing the existing gap in current models that rely on curated content and neighbor information to maintain privacy. An experimental evaluation confirms the efficacy of this approach in outperforming existing models. Additionally, this research provides evidence of the benefits and trade-offs of two evaluation metrics in graph privacy and highlights potential avenues for further research. Furthermore, this study emphasizes the importance of incorporating user-controlled selection methods in graph privacy models. To facilitate reproducibility, the source code for this research is publicly available at https://github.com/jbarridoj/CDGP. This demonstrates the potential of the Content-driven Graph Privacy framework in private content sharing applications and highlights CDGP's performance compared to other state-of-the-art models. An instance of this framework, tailored for academic network research, is also presented along with its benefits and limitations. The atmosphere above the sun's surface holds secrets of energy production and energy release processes that have yet to be fully explained. A major goal of solar research is to determine the minimum amount of energy that enters the corona from the sun's lower layers. Achieving this goal requires instruments that can either look through the corona to measure radiative cooling or detect very low-level energy inputs in the corona. The Focusing Optical Variable Inclined Polarization Observer (FOXSI) on the International Space Station has proven to be effective at doing so by using refractive lenses to focus coronal light on a sensitive camera. FXSII, a second version of the FOXSI instrument, has been proven to be capable of detecting the corona under two different conditions: 1) when it looks through the corona to measure radiative cooling and 2) when it searches for very low-level energy inputs in the corona. The latter capability is particularly important as it has been proven to be able to detect the corona under conditions of solar activity that were previously thought to be too weak to be detected by previous instruments. A major question remains as to whether the low-level energy inputs detected by FOXSII are a result of the dissipation of magnetic fluctuations or instead result from a missing component in current solar models that is not adequately accounting for the corona's energy budget. A key challenge of searching for very low-level energy inputs in the corona is differentiating them from instrumental noise and real solar signals. The project has established a number of criteria that must be met in order for an signal to be classified as a real solar signal and recent observations have met these criteria, indicating that the low-level energy inputs detected by FOXSII are likely to be a real phenomenon. Future plans for the project include searching for very low-level energy inputs in the corona on a wider range of solar objects as well as using the capabilities of FXSII to study other objects such as comets and brown dwarfs. Additionally, the project is working on developing future instruments that will be capable of searching for very low-level energy inputs in the corona more efficiently by focusing on certain spectral ranges that have been previously inaccessible. These future instruments include an instrument concept known as FOXSI-HE, which will be capable of searching for very low-level energy inputs in the corona in a more efficient manner by focusing on certain spectral ranges that have been previously inaccessible. This traditional approach is labor-intensive and makes it challenging to create large, diverse datasets, limiting the ability to develop robust and universally applicable models. Recent advances in machine learning, particularly graph neural networks, hold promise in simplifying this analysis, but existing models struggle with the need for extensive, tailored training datasets. This paper presents a novel approach to create large, realistic datasets through the combination of dataset augmentation and transfer learning. By applying this method, we demonstrate the development of a powerful online community forecasting model using the Twitter platform as an example. Tests using actual policy interventions and field experts as ground truth reveal a notable improvement in prediction accuracy with augmented models, achieving a 38.2% boost in correlation with 82.1% relative absolute error reduction. This research presents a data-driven solution to a long-standing challenge in social media analysis and contributes to the ongoing effort to automate online community forecasting. The proposed method is versatile and can be applied to a broad range of topics, domains, and data types, as evidenced by our policy intervention case studies. We have developed a complete least squares solution for estimating agent positions, taking into account measurement noise and agent positioning errors. This method enhances the accuracy of subsequent estimations for agent velocities, acceleration, and other higher-order dynamics. We have formulated a general approach that can be applied to various systems with time-varying and time-invariant dynamics, as well as developed a specific solution for a fundamental system. We have shown that this method results in lower covariance values for all agents' positions, velocities, and acceleration. We have also provided a method for computing the covariance of agents' positions, velocities, and acceleration. This new solution has been demonstrated to be computationally efficient and compatible with existing 2D multi-agent estimation methods. Our method has been evaluated in an urban driving simulation, where its effectiveness has been verified. Current collaborative filtering methods often overlook the fact that multiple sparse domains coexist in a user's preference profile. This means that even after recommending items in one sparse domain, a user may still have unexpressed preferences in other sparse domains. Our proposed Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation (MSDCR) approach addresses this limitation by developing a novel, unified model that captures cross-interactive relationships across all sparse domains in a user's profile. This involves using a self-attentive mechanism to aggregate item features from different domains based on a user's expressed preferences, and then fine-tuning these aggregates using a multi-task rankers framework to minimize information loss and enhance cooperative recovery. Our experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art baselines, particularly in terms of covering a user's entire profile and improving recommendation performance. Additionally, our theoretical analysis and multiple evaluation metrics validate the MSDCR model's performance and overall effectiveness. Our findings can also be used to guide the construction of explicit preference profiles, as well as inform domain selection strategies in sparse domain adaptation scenarios. When dealing with noisy samples, how can we guarantee that least squares estimation will yield accurate results? To answer this question, we provide a measure of robustness for least squares estimation, expressing the residual of the estimation as a maximum possible quantity based on the standard Euclidean norm. This 'robust' bound is subsequently subdivided into two more specific 'weak' and'strong' bounds, which can be further broken down into quantitative statements applicable to random and worst-case scenarios. Our approach offers two significant advantages over existing methods, as it allows for the presentation of results solely through high-dimensional geometric analysis and provides a general method of obtaining 'robustness' and 'error assurance' bounds for numerous types of estimation problems. Ultimately, we demonstrate that the principles of robustness and error assurance can be utilized to establish a quantitative threshold for the admissibility of estimation procedures. Specifically, we show that least squares estimation will be admissible if the number of samples taken exceeds a particular threshold that is proportional to the degrees of freedom of the model. This 'admissibility' threshold was previously identified by Jimenez et al. under conditions of linearly independent sample data, but our work extends this result to cases of linearly dependent sample data. Current methods for inferring a reward function from observations of an agent's actions, known as inverse reinforcement learning, don't work well when they see the agent navigate partially obstacle-covered spaces. HIRE takes in an agent's trajectory in this type of environment and assumes the agent is trying to maximize a unknown reward function that doesn't change. It breaks down the environment into a series of sub-spaces and uses their geometries, which it learns, to explain the agent's path. This is done by using a model that chooses the most likely set of sub-space geometries that would make the observed actions fit the best. In a similar way, the framework also estimates the bounds of the reward function's influence on what the agent chooses to do next. We tested HIRE on a 2D grid search and a 2D maze, and it turned out that it could pick up on the overall structure of the reward function, even if it only saw the agent's trajectory for a short time. Additionally, the framework's idea of dividing the environment up into separate spaces was also noticeable in the results we got, and we showed that in a situation where we know what the reward function looks like, HIRE can still give us a good idea of its shape. High-entropy alloys, prized for their remarkable strength and flexibility in their composition, are gaining significant attention due to the potential to access and understand mysterious multicomponent phase diagrams. However, experimental and theoretical analyses of these complex systems are hindered by significant challenges, such as high costs, time-consuming procedures, and the inherent uncertainty of predictive modeling. Artificial intelligence and associated techniques have the potential to address these limitations by streamlining sampling processes, enhancing data interpretation with pattern recognition and forecasting capabilities, and refining model construction with the aid of machine learning. This study surveys the progress made so far in the application of machine learning to high-entropy alloys and other similar materials. It then explores the feasibility of using self-learning approaches to uncover hidden secrets in the materials science of high-entropy alloys. Finally, it highlights key difficulties and offers suggestions for further investigation. This article is a summary of the author's presentation at the 2022 TMS Annual Meeting & Exhibition. For the full presentation, please refer to ref. [1].

Recent research in latent variable learning using graph neural networks has focused on untangling cyclic relationships, with applications in predictive and diagnostic medicine. Using differential equations and probabilistic methods, we propose an alternative approach to learning these structures. First, we establish a connection between linear ordinary differential equations and probabilistic Markov random fields. This relationship enables us to use ODEs for predictive tasks, and vice versa. Building on this equivalence, we introduce an ODE-based graph neural network, referred to as the probabilistic and differential equation graph neural network (PDGNN). Furthermore, we develop a method to approximate the underlying Markov random field in a discriminative setting. The proposed PDGNN outperforms previous methods, such as PGGN and GraphSTGN, on predictive and diagnostic medical datasets. The code for our work is available at https://github.com/ytlau/pdgnn. Experimental results demonstrate that PDGNN's probabilistic and differential equation formulations facilitate learning latent variables and directing interventions, which cannot be achieved by previous methods. Additionally, our findings highlight the limitations of current differentiable programming tools for graph neural networks in addressing cyclic structures. A significant reduction in variable size is required to achieve these findings. The empirical evaluation demonstrates the efficacy of our approaches in various clinical and non-clinical latent variable learning applications. Specifically, our models performed well on a diagnostic medical dataset called "medicus", and a deep generative model called "VAE", while also successfully handling directed and cyclic relationships. Furthermore, our work establishes a connection between linear ODEs and MRFs, and explores the integrations and differentiations of these models. The study also introduces an iterative method for solving ODEs, referred to as the "latent variable iteration" (LVI) method. A key aspect of our research is the emphasis on the underlying structural assumptions in graph neural networks. LVI is a novel iterative method for solving ODEs that is informed by the Markov random field's covariance matrix. LVI does not depend on the eigenvalues of this matrix and can be used even when the matrix is singular. In this research, properties related to the structure of finite vector spaces over finite fields are explored, allowing the derivation of lower bounds for the nonlinearity of vectorial Boolean mappings, utilizing measurements that relate to minimal differential weight and slim Sidon sets within the context of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$. Our study showcases the optical frequency comb generator functionality of a microresonator-based system, which can generate multiple spectral lines simultaneously. The mechanism relies on a single pump laser, parametrically exciting the microresonator's eigenfrequencies within a predetermined range. The generated frequency combs exhibit exceptional stability, which makes them suitable for multichannel laser systems requiring high coherence. The microresonator's temperature stability needs to be maintained to a very low level - no more than 50 nanometers in this case - to ensure the precise alignment of the comb's spectral lines. The results reveal a connection between the derived map representation and traditional concepts in geography, such as core areas and peripheral regions, as well as modern theories such as Marx's capitalism analysis and Wallant's France region division. We present a new robust method for detecting widespread patterns of synchronized neuronal activity in small neural networks of inhibitory neurons. This approach, inspired by the ODE schemes in chaos theory, recognizes unique long-lasting dynamics in reduced-order models and is independent of specific network details. Additionally, it corrects for effects of homogeneity and is suitable for large networks. Furthermore, it allows for the extraction of global properties from local dynamics, offering potential applications in neural decoding and network design. This method has been successfully applied to artificial neural networks of inhibitory neurons and has revealed various chimera and synchronization patterns. Furthermore, it has been used to analyze the electrical activity of the nematomorphan worm Caenorhabditis Briggsae. This worm's nervous system consists of 222 homosecretory neurons, arranged in a specific pattern, and displays a wide range of diverse behaviors. By applying our method, the long-term stability of oscillatory and synchronized patterns have been identified and their potential implications on the worm's behavior have been explored. This approach provides a general framework for detecting stable patterns of activity in biological and artificial neural networks. In systems with electronic flat bands, quantum properties such as superconductivity, magnetism, and topological orders are frequently encountered.  Although the flat band's quantum nature is highly desirable, it is often compromised by unfavorable interference from bandwidths that can exist concurrently.  This problem is more acute in multi-atomic systems where the overlap of bandwidths can significantly decrease the flat band's resilience.  Unfortunately, previous studies focusing on flat band-based materials have not adequately addressed this issue, requiring an improved understanding of the relationship between flat bands and concurrent bandwidths.  A recent study involving a Kagome metal, implemented by replacing gold with nickel in the compound PdApT, reveals that an increased number of electrons can either create or destroy the flat band's magnetic ordering, driven by a competition between favoring and suppressing flat band-based magnetism.  This opposing effect is caused by an increased flat band-electron bandwidth that can either complement or contradict the magnetic ordering, resulting in a flat band-related magnetism decline when the bandwidth surpasses a certain threshold.  Moreover, an increased flat band-related magnetism can manifest through long-range ordering or short-range correlations.  A detailed investigation of the electronic structure and magnetic properties of the compound reveals that an increased number of electrons not only create a new bandwidth but also modulate the existing bandwidths, demonstrating that multi-atomic systems can be designed with a new bandwidth that enhances the flat band's resilience.  This design involves a careful selection of atomic replacements that result in a flat band with minimal concurrent bandwidth overlap, thereby increasing the flat band's resilience.  Related theoretical models and experimental findings confirm that an unusual magnetism decline in response to an increased carrier density is a result of flat band interference and demonstrate the potential of Kagome metals in developing flat band-based materials.  These systems can be used in technology due to their unique quantum properties.  A newly suggested family of Kagome metals in the composition PdApX can be designed with a flat band with minimal bandwidth overlap, potentially exhibiting flat band-based magnetism.  A careful selection of atomic replacements can enhance the flat band's resilience in flat band-based materials, as seen in the new member, PdCoS.  This approach may lead to a new class of materials with a new quantum phenomenon if a selected replacement results in a stable flat band.  These findings present a new perspective on flat band design that considers bandwidths in addition to carrier density, offering a more comprehensive understanding of flat band-based materials' quantum nature. This study investigates the performance disparities among clients in federated semi-supervised learning. Recent research has shown that large-scale video understanding tasks can significantly benefit from spatiotemporal alignment, an approach that synchronizes frames in a video according to a pre-defined template. Nonetheless, current alignment methods are limited by their high computational costs, which hinder their application on long-range videos. In response, we present PatchNet, a novel, efficient alignment technique that efficiently matches short-range videos and outperforms existing methods in terms of processing speed. By leveraging a streamlined network architecture, PatchNet achieves a substantial boost in processing speed while still delivering comparable or even improved accuracy compared to other methods. Furthermore, we explore the processing speeds achievable with modern GPU technology, revealing that PatchNet can efficiently handle videos with millions of frames. Our research enables fast and precise alignment of videos, which can be applied to various tasks such as video splitting, merging, and segmentation. Code and model resources are available for reproduction of our results.

Traditional wireless networks may not be able to meet the demands of future multi-service systems, so new research focuses on integrating SWIPT technology into wireless networks to increase user connections and improve data rates. This integration requires considering the effects of power transfer on data transmission and the unique requirements of different applications. Current models typically use a single metric to evaluate the effects of power loss on links and assume a linear relationship between power transfer and node rates, which does not accurately represent the behavior of practical SWIPT systems. In addition, these models often simplify complex applications and fail to account for the interdependence of links in multi-service systems. To address these issues, this study proposes a new model for concurrent multi-user SWIPT systems that takes into account the unique requirements and assumptions of different applications. The findings of this study can be useful in directly and indirectly related fields, such as cognitive radio and MEC, and may require further research to develop these models and the theory of SWIPT. A common pattern in materials research, especially for ferroelectric research, is the use of pseudocubic structures with tetrahedral bonding. Using advanced computer simulations, this study creates a detailed image of the atomic structure in ferroelectric materials with this type of bonding, specifically in the case of strontium titanate and lanthanum titanate. It was discovered that the presence of vacancies in lanthanum titanate significantly affects its atomic structure, leading to a disordered configuration that may contribute to its unique electronic properties. Additionally, this study finds that existing atomic models for these materials are inaccurate and suggests new guidelines for their modification in further research. Finally, this study identifies the potential role of atomic scale defects in the formation of interfaces with adjacent materials, highlighting the importance of clear and accurate visual representations of atomic structures in understanding material properties and behavior in multi-component systems. Overall, this study contributes to a deeper, more detailed understanding of the atomic structure of ferroelectric materials, paving the way for further exploration and application. The findings of this study also have broader implications for the understanding of crystal structure and atomic bonding in minerals and have sparked new hypotheses on the origin and evolution of ferroelectric materials. Specifically, this study raises the question of whether the unique properties of ferroelectric materials are connected to their internal structure and how this, in turn, is linked to their atomic composition. The answers to these questions may lie in the unique configurations of vacancies in lanthanum titanate and other ferroelectric materials with similar properties. Furthermore, this study reveals the potential for ferroelectric materials to be used in cutting-edge technologies, from data storage to quantum computing, and their integration in emerging industries may depend on a more detailed and intuitive understanding of their atomic structure, as revealed in this study. The findings of this research provide a foundational and precise framework for the modification of atomic structures in ferroelectric materials, allowing for further exploration and application. Multivariate data that change over space or time can often be analyzed with a statistical model known as multivariate Gaussian processes (GPs). Researchers have developed new methods by combining multivariate GPs with graphical models, allowing for dependencies between these changing variables to be visualized and analyzed. Two specific approaches, the functional Gaussian graphical framework and graphical GPs, provide different frameworks for understanding relationships between variables and their value over time or in a grid, though they often use similar notation. We establish a geographical duality, referred to as the biduality, for orthomodular lattices. This involves mapping individual elements to geometric shapes, grouping them into basic components called segments, and then reconstructing the lattice structure from these segments. This approach allows us to extend existing duality theories for Boolean and distributive lattices to a broader framework of orthomodular lattices. As a result, we obtain a novel geometric representation of orthomodular lattices, which includes specific applications for finite-dimensional Clifford algebras and certain matrix algebras. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the biduality of orthomodular lattices shares similarities with the geometric duality of positive projective spatio-temporal lattices. Additionally, we explore the association between the geometric duality of orthomodular lattices and the spectral duality of matrix algebras. This research has inspired us to devise a geometric duality for general lattices, which we refer to as the alpha-duality. This method involves dividing a lattice into its upper blocks, establishing a bijective correspondence between these blocks and the upper blocks of the bidual lattice, and demonstrating that the original lattice is isomorphic to a triangular structure formed from the bidual blocks. We have successfully applied the alpha-duality method to various lattices within the categories of finite-dimensonal Clifford algebras and square matrices. This study contributes to the existing literature on duality theories for lattices and provides a useful analytical tool for further exploration of orthomodular lattices and their applications in quantum mechanics and computer science. The main findings of this research are presented in a research paper titled 'Geometrical duality for orthomodular lattices', which includes a detailed proof of the biduality theorem and a comprehensive examination of its consequences and examples. The paper also includes an additional theorem, referred to as the alpha-duality theorem, which outlines the method of geometric duality for general lattices. This method was initially conceived in a previously published article, 'Geometrical duality for lattices'. The results of this research have been jointly presented by the authors at the 2022 CMMPC Conference on Mathematical Physics. The biduality and alpha-duality methods, along with the associated theorems and examples, will be made publicly available through the arXiv platform in a forthcoming paper titled 'Geometrical duality for lattices'. In interior point methods (IPMs), where an iterative method is employed to solve a linear equation system, speeding up convergence often involves developing an effective preconditioner for the linear solver. Our study focuses on the IPM's linear solver, which typically uses a Krylov-based solver such as GMRES. We aim to enhance GMRES' termination criteria to avoid premature restarts by utilizing the residual's norm in the solution space of the primal-dual interior point method. Our proposed modification incorporates an 'almost' termination criterion that estimates the desired error and allows GMRES to terminate early. Our experimental results demonstrate that this modification yields a substantial time savings without compromising accuracy. Specifically, the modified GMRES outperforms standard GMRES in 115 out of 200 tested iterations, accounting for approximately a 25% reduction in total iterations. Furthermore, this enhancement is more pronounced when the interior point method is converged and the linear equation system's coefficient matrix is highly contaminated. Our study does not address the connection to Black Box Interior Point methods but does provide code implementations through GitHub and The Algorithm Library. We encourage further research on this idea, which may be extended to other Krylov solvers and algorithms. By applying this technique to the Gaussian model, we show that it maintains the model's overall structure after the transformation. Additionally, we identify and solve the renormalization group flow equation under the condition that the renormalization constant remains constant, yielding a surprising result: the covariance matrix undergoes geometric transformation specific to the dimension of the field. Furthermore, we propose a novel renormalization group technique known as "Gradient Flow", offering a direct and algorithmic approach to achieve a scale-reduced Quantum Field Theory model. We also explore an algorithmic strategy to extend this method for use in higher-order models. Ultimately, we demonstrate the method's capability to model complex phenomena such as Bonn measurements data with ease. It was successfully able to produce a scale-reduced model for this data without resorting to invasive interventions. We also show that our method produces results consistent with Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods in simulated "Higgs Classification" data while significantly reducing computational costs. Real-world processes often require a blend of these methodologies to capture their full essence. To address this shortcoming, our previous work introduced a novel process model called HPBM (Hybrid Process Business Model), which can model business processes using multiple paradigms in conjunction. However, ensuring that actual process executions align with the specified hybrid process model is a challenging task. In this paper, we develop an automata-theoretic framework to formalize the hybrid process model and define the acceptable region, or language, of feasible process instances. We also explore the creation of monitors to enforce the hybrid process model constraints during process operation, enabling the detection of process deviations and facilitating model-based business process management. In particular, our framework enables the identification of infeasible process activities, allowing for corrective actions and the avoidance of process failures. We illustrate our monitor's effectiveness through a practical case study in the context of dispute management. The experimental results of this empirical study confirm the monitor's correctness and showcase its practical applications in business process management. The proposed monitor offers a practical solution to enforce the hybrid process model constraints, thereby contributing to the development of business process-oriented systems. Additionally, this study demonstrates the practical utility of business process-oriented methods in real-world scenarios. Based on these findings, we advocate for the integration of business process-oriented methods into current process management paradigms to cover all possible use cases. Its effectiveness stems from the abstract semantic interpretation of circuit descriptions facilitating the transformation and adaptation of programs. However, the scope of Quipmer, the high-level version of Quipper, is limited by the absence of support for nested substitutions within its existing semantics. Thus, a new conceptual machine-based semantics for Quipmer is introduced, addressing this gap and allowing for the efficient evaluation of complex quantum programs. Additionally, the introduced semantics serves as a foundation for further modifications and extensions of the Quipmer language. A demonstration of the newly designed conceptual machine semantics in operation has been rendered online accessible. Furthermore, the implementation of an associated prototype-based interpreter has been completed. Using this tool, the verification of the correctness of the implementation in Quipmer against the original Quipper framework has been accomplished. Consequently, the enhanced conceptual machine semantics provides a viable solution for handling nested substitutions in Quipmer, thereby opening up the potential for further enhancements to the Quipmer language. In this study, we have modelled a two-dimensional percolation model using random matrices with occupation probability distributed according to the power-law pattern as the matrix size increases. We found that the distribution of the extreme values within this model transitions from a Gaussian distribution for small matrix sizes to a heavier-tailed distribution, specifically a Cauchy distribution, for larger matrix sizes. We have also observed that the probability of this shift occurring is dependent on the threshold at which the extreme values are measured and found to be associated with a diverging characteristic size of the extreme regions. This behaviour is similar to that observed in the massive phase of a semiconducting polymer and can be characterized by a scaling exponent of 0.63. Furthermore, we have developed a field theory to describe this model and the resulting distributions of extreme values, and have used this theory to calculate the corrections to these distributions for small matrix sizes. These corrections take the form of a logarithmic correction in two dimensions, an result consistent with previous findings on the Kesten random walk. We have verified the accuracy of our field theory by demonstrating that the predictions made by this theory are in good agreement with the results of our numerical simulations. These results provide a basis for understanding how distributions of extreme values may change in response to variations in the underlying disorder of a system, and the resulting effects on the scaling and critical behaviour of these distributions. The emergence of single-molecule, long-read sequencing technologies has revolutionized genome assembly but sequencing these genomes directly is impractical due to the massive number of overlapping reads. Constructing a draft genome from short-reads is a more feasible initial approach, and then using long-reads to improve and refine the assembly. However, scaling this process to construct multiple genomes efficiently is a significant challenge. We've developed the parallel genome constructor (PGC) software to address this issue, and in this study, we've refined PGC to efficiently handle large-scale sequencing projects by distributing the assembly process across multiple CPUs. Our optimizations enable PGC to construct genomes from thousands of sequencing runs simultaneously, and our results show a near-linear scaling of computational resources to meet the needs of modern genome and crop genome consortia, and even allows for the construction of a complete human genome in a distributed environment. Our research demonstrates the significant potential of PGC in addressing the needs of genome consortiums for accurate and reliable genome assembly services. Text recognition in structured documents such as tickets, IDs, and forms often involves extracting specific pattern-based information. However, current methods tend to overlook key pieces of data, particularly if they fail to recognize the layout or identify the critical characters within the text. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach called RegFavoring, which prioritizes the detection of patterns essential for accurate extraction. By integrating the priorities set by human experts with the likelihood of character recognition, RegFavoring optimizes the matching process on a structured text recognition dataset. Our results demonstrate improved extraction rates of over 12% and 5.75% respectively, along with a significant reduction of nearly 66% in errors compared to a leading layout analysis method. You can explore the performance of our approach on the CamV2 dataset here. This website provides a detailed analysis of recognized texts, along with accurate extraction rates for both layout and text components. Importantly, it highlights instances where our method excels in extracting specific keywords, underscoring the importance of incorporating prior knowledge in enhancing the overall effectiveness of structured text recognition. To evaluate the impact of prioritizing certain patterns on recognition accuracy, we introduce the Prioritize Char Error Rate (Pcher). Our calculation shows a substantial decrease of more than 5.75% in this error rate when comparing RegFavoring with a leading analysis method. You can find our full code and demo at this repository. Our approach aims to contribute to the ongoing development of state-of-the-art methods in structured text recognition, particularly in identifying critical characters for accurate extraction. By addressing both recognition and error metrics, RegFavoring facilitates the continued optimization and refinement of existing models. Furthermore, regfavoring's priority learning mechanism may find applications in tasks such as named entity recognition, where extracting specific entities involves identifying characteristic based patterns. To illustrate this point, we analyzed the CamV2 dataset and discovered that human priors on specific patterns in names and addresses are often neglected by current methods, leading to a significant decrease in extraction rates. To address this gap, regfavoring's error rates can inform the development of enhanced models that incorporate prior knowledge. semantic and syntactic elements, by crossing these characteristics with
table-centric dialects of SQL. We found that prior approaches overlooked
table descriptions, compromising their translation abilities. To address this, we
developed a comprehensive end-to-end model that translates English into SQL

semantic analysis and a type of language model and language modeling to grasp
syntactic details. Furthermore, we introduced a column selection task to
augment SQL generation. Experimental results show that our proposed model
significantly improves performance over state-of-the-art methods on diverse
datasets, spanning various domains, with a notable boost of 19.5% on average

The first approach utilizes the traditional, slow-changing methodology that involves calculating the rate of entropy production based on the system's relaxation rate and deviation from thermal equilibrium. This approach can be challenging with experimental data in hand, particularly if the relaxation rate is unknown. An alternative method involves using a system that changes rapidly but slowly compared to its natural relaxation time, effectively validating the entropy production rate as a conservative quantity that is consistent with the second law of thermodynamics. This approach leverages the Asymptotic Chaos Theory (ACT) framework, allowing for entropy production to be calculated directly from experimental data without requiring knowledge of the system's detailed mechanics. This new analysis reveals a striking correlation with a known entropy production rate metric, further demonstrating ACT's utility in testing the second law of thermodynamics in non-equilibrium systems. Most importantly, ACT's methodology is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of systems that undergo rapid change, paving the way for third-law-like applications that utilize entropy production rather than entropy loss. Research has focused on analyzing and interpreting the results of procedure monitoring, which assesses the implementation of process guidelines. In contrast, little is known about evaluating the actual process itself. This paper offers a comparative analysis of process evaluation and the analysis of process recordings, identifying key considerations and potential solutions. The authors introduce a flexible and adaptable framework for procedural monitoring that can be applied to diverse processes and present an empirical study involving this framework's application to two distinct processes: one technological and one social. This study explores participants' reactions to procedural monitoring and examines the relationship between process evaluation and monitoring. The results indicate that participants are generally positive about being monitored but wary of outside evaluation. The findings also suggest that procedural monitoring and process evaluation are intertwined and capable of mutual enrichment. Moving forward, the authors suggest combining these two aspects to foster a more collaborative and productive atmosphere in future studies. A collaborative approach could also lead to more successful interactions between humans and intelligent systems. This study's findings and the proposed framework can be utilized by researchers as a guide for analyzing and interpreting procedure monitoring and process data. Additionally, the results may be applied by practitioners as a means of enhancing their understanding of these phenomena and making more informed decisions, especially in practical settings. The authors stress the need for more diverse and many-sided studies on these topics in the future. A repository with all the used code is available at https://github.com/jasecl/procedure-monitoring and the videos of the studied participants can be found at https://jasecl.github.io/procedure-monitoring/. The data collected during the study is available at https://jasecl.github.io/procedure-monitoring/data/. Over the past 15 years, the compressing power of the Burrows-Wheeler Transform (BWT) has made it a widely accepted solution to various algorithmic challenges. Although the BWT is an efficient compressor, its inverse can be computationally expensive. Researchers have proposed multiple approaches to overcome this limitation; however, most of these solutions are dependent on the available space or memory. Rasmus Pagh and Søren Nyvang Andersen introduced a space-efficient algorithm known as Fast Compressed Follow-by-K-Mer Counting (FastCBKMC) in 2013, which utilizes the BWT of a text's suffix tree to count occurrences of a k-mer within a given range of occurrences in the text. However, the current fastest algorithm for this problem has a time complexity of O(n log^2 n) and relies on the output of the BWT's follow sorting order. We present a new approach, the Stacking Algorithm, which efficiently calculates the follow sorting order for the BWT of a text with a time complexity of O(n) and a space complexity of O(n N) where n and N represent the text and its longest repeating substring lengths, respectively. This algorithm provides a novel application of the stacking structure, a data structure we introduced for suffix tree automation, enabling the creation of the first linear-time algorithm for the FastCBKMC problem. Additionally, we introduce three new kernelization problems for the fast counting issue. Our first kernelization problem, the FCBKMC problem, emerges from the FastCBKMC issue with the additional constraint of equal occurrence counts for a given k-mer within a text. It involves determining if a given k-mer occurs more frequently in one part of a text as it does in another part. When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of fluids and suspensions undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, a phenomenon known as shear thickening that can lead to catastrophic reductions in viscosity. Despite decades of research, the causes and consequences of shear thickening remain poorly understood, particularly in complex suspensions that can cause it. A new scaling law for shear thickening transitions is presented, derived from a theory originally designed to handle slow, entangled polymers. By applying it to suspensions with high-stress impurities, the model demonstrates a broader applicability than its underlying theory, yielding a single, universal power law for all shear thickening suspensions. A thorough evaluation against a broad array of suspension data reveals excellent agreement, spanning multiple mechanisms and types of suspensions, with even weaker and less dense suspensions still adhering to the original polymer model. This leads to an estimation of when shear thickening begins in even thinner suspensions, and raises the possibility of analogous transitions in less dense, particle-based fluids. Moreover, the model is integrated with a state diagram, offering a new and complex geometry to describe and classify different rheological states, and highlighting the connection between shear thickening and other extreme rheological phenomena. Finally, the study proposes that shear thickening may signify a general, catastrophic failure of fluid continuity, and that dense and less dense suspensions, high-stress fluids, and slow polymers share a common, intricate physics, with the transition to these states signifying a profound, multifaceted shift in the behavior of matter. This research opens up several avenues for further exploration and clarifies several underlying principles, shedding new light on the underlying physics of shear thickening and its corresponding rheological states. Building on these methods and findings, the researchers propose a new approach to evaluate the overall richness of results from modern search platforms. The core issue with developing photovolatiles on terrestrial planets as a theory for their depletion at close-in ages to giant planet formation is the need to identify planets of suitable size and orbital path from existing data. Current research uses radial velocity measurements to gather relevant data, with a key characteristic of suitable planets being their mass between that of Neptune and Saturn. To uncover this information, scientists analyze the properties of known exoplanets from relevant studies. This is particularly true for planets in close orbit to their host stars, with a focus on those discovered using specific techniques and samples. Researchers previously found that many sub-Saturn-mass planets are destroyed by migrating giant planets in a particular survey. They later extended their research to the CORALIE/HARPS radial velocity program, analyzing a different set of discovered planets. Our analysis indicates that the correlation between planet destruction and giant planets found in previous studies does not hold for the CORALIE/HARPS sample. Using statistical analysis on the properties of discovered planets, scientists found no evidence to support the theory that photovolatiles are depleted on terrestrial planets in close orbit to giant planets. This is reflected in the destruction of such planets by migrating giants. Our analysis also demonstrates that the CORALIE/HARPS survey has a higher detection threshold for smaller planetary masses when considering its sampling density and discovery techniques. As a result, it has a more comprehensive view of the destroyed planet population in close orbit to giant planets. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that the destroyed planet population in close orbit to giant planets is not solely the result of single giant planet masses but rather a range of masses from 0.3 to 4 times that of Jupiter. Our findings also have implications for the use of radial velocity techniques and the analysis of other planetary systems, with a key consideration being the detection thresholds of such techniques and how they affect the view of the destroyed planet population. Our analysis also underscores the significance of diversity in the methods and techniques used to gather data and the necessary consideration for detection thresholds in such research. Based on our statistical analysis and the properties of discovered planets, scientists estimate that up to 30% of planets with a mass between that of Neptune and Saturn in the CORALIE/HARPS sample are in close orbit to giant planets and retain their atmospheric volatiles. It does this by optimizing a new objective function that promotes a more compact and interconnected attention map, thereby enhancing the network's ability to learn and generalize. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a set of well-established benchmark tests in the fields of NLP and image classification, resulting in superior performance and broader generalization of the model. Our implementation of TARSIM is available on GitHub under the name "TARSIM". Additionally, we have conducted a study that showcases the influence of different model characteristics on the diversity of generated attention maps, which can be accessed through an interactive visualization tool. We have also proposed a new metric for evaluating the connectivity of attention maps, specifically the Specificity metric, which can be utilized in various applications of machine learning. Furthermore, we have conducted an analysis of the internal workings of the model and observed a correlation between the connectivity of attention maps and the model's ability to learn and generalize. Our research has several significant applications in the field of machine learning, ranging from the interpretation of model decisions to the acceleration of inference processes, and we have also explored these aspects in greater detail. We investigate the compressed dark sector in models featuring a Yukawa interaction between dark matter particles. This model is characterized by a simple gauge singlet Yukawa coupling, which generates a mass proportional to the standard model Higgs field. The highly compressed nature of dark matter arises from a near-degenerate mass spectrum, which is possible due to a Yukawa coupling that is not sensitive to the standard model Higgs field's temperature. Our analysis focuses on the specific case of a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetric model, in which we find that a compressed dark matter mass range of $10^{-10}$ to $10^{-6}$ GeV is feasible. This is distinct from more conventional halo dark matter models, which typically result from a halo formation process. Our analysis further reveals that the simple, singular nature of the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry may be replaced by more complex symmetry frameworks, such as the $\mathbb{Z}_N$ symmetry, which would lead to even more compressed dark matter models. The lower bound on the $\mathbb{Z}_N$ symmetry rank, N, is determined to be 3, as it would lead to an irreparable disruption of halo structure due to the resulting high degree of dark matter compression. Our work thus establishes a comprehensive understanding of the $\mathbb{Z}_N$ symmetry, as well as the resulting properties of the compressed dark matter model. Additionally, we point out that the simple, singular $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry can be replaced by more general models, such as the modular invariant symmetry, in which we find that the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry is preferred due to its ability to resolve the Higgs window. However, we also identify a residual impact of the modular symmetry on the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ model, which may lead to further dark matter candidates beyond the simple, singular model. Finally, we illustrate the practical utility of our theoretical findings by investigating the convergence of iterative global averaging algorithms. Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation benefits from pre-training, a crucial step in object detection and segmentation tasks. Traditionally, models are pre-trained on image classification tasks. This study examines alternative pre-training methods for segmentation task models, specifically comparing traditional classification and two-depth assessment approaches, which evaluate scene characteristics in an anatomical or spatial structure. Our analysis reveals that classification and two-depth assessment pre-training are not universally beneficial and depend on the specific scene representation and sensor modalities used. Notably, classification pre-training may degrade anatomically-organized scene representations, while two-depth assessment pre-training may harm models using multi-modal sensor data. Crucially, our findings suggest that depth assessment pre-training can enhance segmentation task performance when sensor data is single-modal, a common scenario in practical applications. This study introduces a novel pre-training approach, adaptively selecting between classification and depth assessment for better anatomical scene representations. Our method surpasses traditional classification pre-training on the KITTI dataset by 3.6% in terms of categorical IoU. Additionally, this study showcases two-depth assessment pre-training's superiority over classification pre-training on the NYU-V2 dataset by 4.1%, as well as introduces an alternative 3D depth assessment task and corresponding model. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/asharman/depth_assessment_pretraining. This study delves into an unexplored area of deep neural network pre-training for semantic segmentation and provides insights into the relative benefits of classification and depth assessment tasks. As such, it is anticipated that this work will contribute to the ongoing discussion in the community. Additionally, it is expected that future research will build upon these findings, particularly with respect to depth assessment, and potentially lead to the development of more effective pre-training methods. Traditional approaches to video narration and time-series forecasting often rely on rule-based methods. However, these techniques are inflexible and can't be adapted to tell videos with different contexts or to incorporate new data. There's also a limitation in using only rule-based methods to generate time-series data in various scenarios. This can result in wearisome storytelling that fails to engage the listener. This paper introduces TCube, a model that uses neural networks to create time-series data and tells engaging stories in video narration and time-series forecasting. TCube models the relationships between time-series data and tells coherent, interactive stories that outperform existing methods in various domains. It also shows promise in the domain of video narration by describing the key events in a video with more detail and context. TCube's ability to tell stories in different domains and to handle new data comes from its capacity to learn domain-agnostic patterns. This learning is facilitated by TCube's use of a multi-head attention mechanism that allows it to prioritize relevant time-series data when generating the story. TCube's performance in time-series forecasting is enhanced by its use of a multi-step mechanism that allows it to predict future data by mimicking its neighbors. TCube's stories are also shown to be more accurate and engaging when generated using this mechanism. TCube's primary limitation is its lack of stories about specific events in its training data. This is a legacy of existing methods for time-series data and can be addressed by supplementing TCube with raked data. TCube's potential to improve video narration and time-series forecasting was demonstrated in experiments conducted on various datasets. TCube's source code is publicly available. The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has analyzed real-time data to search for anomalies in beauty meson behavior, particularly focusing on the areas of CP violation, rare decays, and electroweak precision tests. By leveraging these studies, the experiment aims to gain insights into the properties of the weak interaction and its impact on matter composition. This research paper outlines the methods used by the ATLAS collaboration to investigate these phenomena, detailing various analysis techniques, results, and findings. The ATLAS data have enabled the creation of the most restrictive constraints to date on several rare decay processes and CP violation phenomena.
