Our investigation focuses on the stability of dark solitons in the mean-field regime of nonlinear Schr\"{o}dinger equations, particularly with intensity-dependent dispersion, where the nonlinearity and dispersion coefficients are proportional to $|u|^2$ and $\int |u|^4 dx$, respectively. We demonstrate that, unlike in the case of linear dispersion, where stability is determined solely by the soliton's initial perturbation and not its shape, introducing non-linear dispersion results in dark solitons with large soliton areas exhibiting increased stability. This increased stability is caused by a cross-talk effect between the soliton and the surrounding radiation, which is made possible by the non-linear dispersion. This phenomenon is observed in both one-dimensional and two-dimensional models. Moreover, we analyze the expanded spectral stability criterion and find that non-linear dispersion reduces the minimum eigenvalue of the spectral stability problem compared to linear dispersion. This finding is corroborated by numerical simulations of the ordinary differential equation generated from the non-linear Schr\"{o}dinger equation, thus highlighting the significance of considering the mean-field regime in both conservative and dissipative settings. Furthermore, we explore the obtained results in the context of 1D saturable Bose-Einstein condensates, illustrating the altered dynamics through simulations of the Hamiltonian mean-field equations. In AE, we see altered dark soliton dynamics, particularly noting the emergence of accelerated dark solitons in the absence of linear dispersion. Additionally, we investigate how well our theoretical findings align with the results obtained from the full quantum model, thus ultimately enabling the generation of spatial solitons with large areas. These solitons are conserved in the mean-field regime but become stable in the conserved regime. In BE, we see accelerated dark solitons in the mean-field regime but note their instability in the conserved regime. Moreover, we examine the obtained results in the context of 2D saturable Bose-Einstein condensates, thus ultimately enabling the generation of dark solitons with large areas. In this regard, we analyze the survival of dark solitons in 2D saturable Bose-Einstein condensates through the solution of the Hamiltonian flow equation obtained from the 2D nonlinear Schr\"{o}dinger equation. The results are compared against those obtained from the full quantum model, thus ultimately enabling the generation of dark solitons with large areas. Our approach introduces Lotse, a structure that generates direction-based guidance for exploratory visual data analysis. It consists of three key elements: guides, targets, and fields. Guides provide general direction, withstood by targets serving as concrete examples, while fields enable users to delve into underlying details. This integrative framework fosters a systematic method for developing direction-based recommendations, as demonstrated through two practical applications of this method. One example incorporates Lotse within existing methodology as a direction-aware assistant, as seen in SHAP. The other exemplifies Lotse as a direction-based language for describing and combining different visual guidance methods, as illustrated in Guided. The evaluation of Lotse's efficacy through user studies confirms that it supplements users' abilities to form meaningful insights and conducts more focused and efficient visual analysis. Furthermore, Lotse's practicality is underscored by its integration into Guided, a widely used tool with over 400,000 users, where it has replaced a core component and facilitated significant improvements in user engagement and analysis quality. Lotse's source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/danielwieland/lotse. Currently, Lotse supports direction-based guidance in XAML-based Visual Studio projects and C#; efforts are underway to extend its support to Java and Eclipse. Lotse holds promise as a general direction-based guidance structure, encompassing various applications and methodologies within the field of visual data analysis. Its underlying theory and algorithmic framework may be adapted to provide direction-based guidance in numerous other contexts, such as recommendation systems and multimedia search. In particular, Lotse's direction-based guidance methodology exhibits similarities with knowledge graph embeddings, which could serve as a potential area for further exploration and extension of Lotse's capabilities. Lotse's evaluation through user studies reveals the positive impact of direction-based guidance on the efficiency and quality of visual data analysis. Its integration into Guided, a widely used tool, has led to substantial gains in user engagement and analysis quality. Consequently, Lotse may serve as a useful addition to existing methodologies in visual data analysis, including but not limited to Guided, SHAP and other tools, where it could improve direction-based guidance and enhance the overall analysis experience. Lotse's direction-based guidance, encapsulated within the Lotse structure, fosters a systematic method for developing and combining different guidance approaches, as seen in its application in SHAP and Guided. The underlying theory and algorithmic framework of Lotse may be adapted to provide direction-based guidance in various contexts, such as recommendation systems and multimedia search.

A novel coil design, referred to as the QBox coil, has been developed with the versatility to produce a range of magnetic configurations, including quasi-helical torus, stellarators, and tokamak scenarios, all with minimal variation in magnetic configuration. The stellarator variant of the QBox coil has been optimized and demonstrated to achieve notable achievements such as a reduced variation in magnetic configuration (less than 0.05%), a magnetic field smoothness of 6.4 milligaus per radius, and a tri-axial elastic deformation constant of 1.1. The flow of heat within a stationary bed of spheres is being studied by comparing computational models to experimental data obtained using rapid Magnetic Resonance Imaging. This imaging technique enabled us to observe the velocity and temperature of fluid (water in this case) as it flows through a bed of glass spheres with a specific porosity of 0.64. We found that the experiments align with the predictions made by the Dukovic correlation, which describes the thermal distribution in an isotropic packed bed. The agreement between the experimental and computational results indicates that the Dukovic correlation can be applied even in cases where the correlation length is comparable to the diameter of the particles. Additionally, we observed that the thermal conductivity of the packbed is reduced due to an absence of convection, and this reduction in conductivity is dependent on the temperature difference and fluid velocity. We also found that the temperature distribution within the packbed is characterized by a non-linear gradient, particularly in cases where the packbed is probed from the sides, as opposed to being probed from above. This research has identified new areas for further investigation. Furthermore, we believe that Magnetic Resonance Imaging can be an effective tool for obtaining detailed insights into the physics taking place within complex systems. The capabilities of MRI have been demonstrated by our study, and we anticipate that this imaging technique will continue to be essential in understanding phenomena in complex systems for a long time to come. This study aims to bridge this knowledge gap by detailing the development of two multilevel preconditioners: MEA2 and ELA2. These preconditioners ensure consistency with the flexible solvers already available in FEniCS, with MEA2 corresponding to the "Stokes-Alterman" and ELA2 to the "Euler-Alterman" variants. Comprehensive numerical tests on cardiovascular models with stochastic loads validate the effectiveness and scalability of these preconditioners. Notably, the MEA2 variant exhibits superior performance on the "stark" model, while the ELA2 variant performs better on the "starry night" model. These results are later expanded upon to introduce two new variants: MEA3 and ELA3, with three levels instead of two. The corresponding C++ code for these preconditioners is freely accessible on GitHub, enabling potential modifications and adaptations by the community. Ultimately, the decision on an optimal preconditioner hinges on the specific model being used, and we provide a brief strategy on choosing the suitable MEAn and ELAn families based on the characteristics of the system being solved. We examine the long-term behavior of a particular solution method for the two-dimensional compressible FENE dumbbell model, which describes the flow of a viscoelastic fluid. The proposed solution, which accounts for both stochastic forces and external forces, exhibits robust stability in the presence of small random disturbances. A global-in-time error estimate for this solution method is established, showing that it converges to a specific equilibrium state on a longer timescale. Importantly, our estimate is independent of the initial data, allowing us to analyze the long-term behavior of this solution method in more detail. Specifically, our results indicate that a particular timescale derived from the Omega lemma influences the long-term behavior of this solution method, which has also been verified through numerical simulations based on the coexistence of multiple stable modes in the model. By contrast, our approach does not rely on any assumption regarding the frequency or structure of these modes. Rather, our results emerge from a detailed analysis of the straining vortex, which reveals a direct connection between these modes and the timescales identified in the model. Furthermore, our work implies that certain long-term properties of the solution, such as convergence to a specific equilibrium state and the tracking of an approximate solution, may also apply to more complex models, including the Maxwell model and the Bingham model. A corresponding discussion of these generalizations is included in the main text. Additionally, our approach highlights the potential of global-in-time error estimates to shed new light on the underlying dynamics of the model by addressing questions of timescale selection and the long-term behavior of one-dimensional solutions. Several suggestions for pursuing this line of inquiry are included in the main text. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain in obtaining widespread practical applications. Reinforcement learning solutions frequently fail to generalize to new tasks or progressively learn multiple skills throughout a lifetime of learning. In contrast, a lifelong reinforcement learning approach is capable of overcoming these challenges, but evaluating its effectiveness presents significant difficulties due to the lack of standardized benchmarks that model real-life conditions of learning from experience. To address this issue, we introduce an open-source platform called L2Explorer that incorporates various benchmarks and tools to evaluate the performance of lifelong reinforcement learning methods. Our environment encompasses a diverse range of basic tasks as well as more complex scenarios, all designed to simulate real-life conditions of learning. Additionally, we utilize this platform to investigate the performance of a fundamental agent that adheres to the principles of episodic memory, and our analysis highlights the potential for an agent that learns through experience to achieve superior outcomes in both simple and complex settings. The COVID-19 pandemic in South Africa was characterized by a two-month delay in data reporting, rendering publicly available information incomplete. This study utilized publicly postible datasets, including Twitter, Wikipedia page views, and Google Trends to comprehend the epidemic's progression in South Africa. These datasets, combined with existing time-series data from Public Health England, enabled a comprehensive understanding of the epidemic. This was further supplemented by using Wikipedia page views to estimate time-series data for provinces, as well as by validating the analysis through cross-validation. The findings from this analysis align with official time-series data from Public Health England, demonstrating the effectiveness of using Wikipedia to forecast the epidemic's progression in different provinces. The Twitter data contributed to detecting the pandemic's onset, while Google Trends played a minor role. The integration of these accessible datasets facilitated monitoring the epidemic in South Africa's provinces even during data shortages. The methodology employed in this study can serve as a guideline for utilizing accessible data to complement official time-series data to enhance Public Health England's insights. Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally posits that if subsets A and B, having a sum-set with cardinality n, are respectively comprised of m-element and k-element integers, then A + B can be contained within a set with at most cn powers of 2, where the constant c is approximately 4.104. In this study, we seek to enhance this outcome by reducing the constant. Our investigation reveals that the existing 4.104 upper limit can be lowered to 4.077. To accomplish this, we incorporate an altered version of the Erdős-Szemerédi sum set problem into our reasoning, alongside a novel application of Bentley's algorithm to the additive combinatorics domain. Ultimately, our method gives rise to a novel additive Freiman's 3k-4 theorem variant. In addition, this method enables the creation of an intuitive, graphical helper tool, known as a 'delta set computer,' which facilitates the computation of Freiman's 3k-4 theorem-related issues. Consequently, the key challenges of Freiman's 3k-4 theorem can be solved using our proposed tool. In particular, it enables the determination of the smallest possible size of a set that contains all sums of pairs of elements from a given subset of integers, which has the potential to yield new insights into the additive Erdős-Szemerédi sum set problem. In this context, our research tool presents a significant enhancement of the known lower bound, specifically 2^18, which was previously established by Ben Green. Following the submission of our work, the lower bound was further enhanced to 2^20 by Gower and Ruszczyński. Nonetheless, our method continues to hold as a valid approach to solving the additive Erdős-Szemerédi sum set problem. Major ophthalmic disorders, such as glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy, are escalating in importance due to their connection to common conditions like increased eye pressure and sugar issues in the blood. Effective identification and monitoring of these diseases are crucial for maintaining eye health, yet current methods are often time-consuming, expensive, or require extensive expertise. An approach called multimodal deep learning has shown significant potential in improving disease detection and diagnosis by integrating multiple image types, such as standard eye images and OCT scans, to enhance accuracy and operational efficiency. An integrated dataset of 351,150 images from various sources was created and divided into training and testing sets to test the performance of this approach. An improved method called the CoTrNet architecture achieved better results on classification tasks related to glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy by evaluating eye health more comprehensively. An assessment of this approach on a competition dataset demonstrated its superiority over current methods, resulting in a 2.7% improvement in AUC and 3.4% improvement in top-1 accuracy. Additionally, the trained models showed resilience to various forms of interference and performed well on distinct datasets with a minimal drop in performance. The eye health toolkit, including the integrated dataset and processing code, has been made available for other researchers to build upon. An analysis of the benefits and limitations of this approach suggests that multimodal deep learning can contribute significantly to maintaining eye health by using advanced technology to support medical specialists. An evaluation of the potential impact of this approach on ophthalmology revealed its potential to improve diagnosis and treatment of various eye disorders, ultimately leading to better patient outcomes. This research explores the theoretical and numerical aspects of identifying the boundary of a domain where transmission eigenvalue problems occur, specifically in the context of centrally symmetric materials. Initially, we establish a proof of uniqueness for the identified boundary under assumed 'outer' regime conditions. Next, we introduce a iterative algorithm based on the Lasso method to recover the boundary, particularly designing it for the 'inner' regime due to its simplified requirements. Finally, a convex optimization approach drives the recovery process, aided by a semismooth Newton-Fermat algorithm for resolution. Notably, our methods introduce new markers and adaptative algorithms to facilitate efficient computation of the boundary under various types of differentiation. The study also introduces a model problem formulation and provides a first-order convergence analysis for the iterative algorithm. To validate our findings, a set of numerical examples are implemented and analyzed under different 'inner' and 'outer' scenarios, exhibiting good agreement between the proposed algorithm and the exact boundary. Ultimately, our methods offer promising insights into recovering the boundary under various types of differentiation. However, further research is required to achieve robust performance across a diverse set of functions. The study is available in full at the arXiv website under the identifier 2207.06510. In an attempt to overcome limitations in current intent detection methods that often require a prior knowledge of intents, we propose a new approach called NLPRing+. It employs a dual-module architecture: (1) a pre-trained deep set network for identifying similarities among unlabelled intent data and generating semi-supervised labels, and (2) a contrastive learning module that learns representations compatible with labelled data by matching similar intent groups. By maintaining semi-similar and contrastive properties of representations, NLPRing+ effectively detects novel intents while preserving labelled intent classifications. Experimental evaluations on two datasets demonstrate the superior performance of NLPRing+ over state-of-the-art techniques in both novel intent detection and non-target intent detection tasks. Additionally, NLPRing+ maintains high accuracy in traditional intent classification tasks, exemplifying its ability to improve performance on both unsupervised and supervised settings. All source code and datasets used in this research are publicly accessible at https://github.com/david-ding-uc/NLPRingplus.

The notion of a simplicial group can be defined through various methods, such as the extension of a simplicial ring to a graded ring or the application of the simplicial Dold-Kan functor to the category of simplicial abelian groups. However, our main finding reveals that a global simplicial bundle can be viewed as a simplicial group in its entirety, rather than just a group that can be obtained from a local sequence. Furthermore, the images of the functors $\Delta_*\mathbb{Z}$ and $\Sigma_*\mathbb{Z}$ are comprised of the simplicial groups that satisfy $\pi_0X=\mathbb{Z}$, with $\pi_1X$ also being a global simplicial bundle. Additionally, the functors $\Delta_*\mathbb{Z}$ and $\Sigma_*\mathbb{Z}$ represent two sides of the same simplicial spectrum, with $\mathbb{Z}$ representing the ground ring in both instances. Ultimately, our discovery demonstrates that the simplicial groups with a trivial zeroth homotopy group form a simplicial spectrum, with $\mathbb{Z}$ being the ring that generates it. This result can be viewed as a generalization of Milnor's theorem. The proof involves the reconstruction of a global simplicial bundle from the homological properties of a simplicial group with a trivial zeroth homotopy group. This approach is akin to the method used by Dold and Lefschetz to determine the homotopy groups of a sphere. By doing so, we provide a proof of the simplicial version of the Milnor theorem. The proposed method has the potential to be applied to other theorems in homotopy theory, enabling the derivation of their simplicial versions. The problem of visual relationship detection aims to identify connections between objects within images. A key challenge in this task is reducing false positives - incorrect relationships between objects. In this study, we examine the source of the false positive issue and propose a new assessment metric that helps alleviate this problem. This metric, called the Area Under the Response Curve, gives higher weight to predictions that are consistently correct, even at low confidence levels. When using the AP metric in training, we find that models become more accurate and less prone to false positives. Specifically, the models' false positive rate decreases by 69% on the VCOPs dataset. This improvement is made possible by a pre-trained backbone that utilizes layout information to help the models distinguish between correct and incorrect relationships. Additionally, we propose a new dataset called PHAIR, which contains 1,111 human-annotated labels that help to further refine the models' performance and reduce false positives. Our approach achieves superior results on the VCOPs dataset, outperforming other state-of-the-art methods in nearly all metrics. Notably, the models' overall accuracy and adversarial robustness also increase as a result of using the AP metric. Our code and dataset are available for public use at the provided link. The feeble measurement has emerged as a breakthrough in quantum measurement theory, offering a straightforward method to analyze quantum states within the context of trace metrics. However, its connection to real-world measurement devices remains unclear. To address this issue, we investigate the quantum connection cost (QCC) - a novel error minimization approach for the feeble measurement. Our study reveals that the QCC provides a more accurate prediction of measurement errors compared to other methods. Importantly, we demonstrate that the QCC can be expressed as the maximum trace error between the density matrix and a probability-weighted average of pure states, thereby gaining insight into its effectiveness. Furthermore, we show that the QCC can be computed using a parallel algorithm, enabling efficient evaluations. Our practical assessments using random quantum states confirm that the QCC surpasses the optimal performance of other methods. Moreover, we link the QCC to the generalized quantum measurement framework, establishing its relevance to real-world measurements. Our work, encompassing theoretical analysis and practical testing, showcases the quantum connection cost as a powerful tool for quantum state analysis and guidance of measurement procedures. The emergence of social media has led to an unprecedented amount of online human interactions, generating vast datasets that have facilitated significant breakthroughs in social computing research. However, the current approach to modeling social networks is often flawed, as it is based on ad-hoc methods that neglect to provide a comprehensive understanding of the used data and algorithms. In this context, we introduce COMNET, a complete social network generator that we developed to create accurate representations of online social relationships, as demonstrated through an in-depth analysis of Google+ datasets. By evaluating various metrics, COMNET has been shown to surpass existing methods in terms of precision and recall, while its suitability for machine learning tasks has been validated through experiments using multiple models. The source code for COMNET is freely available at https://github.com/Chen-chen/GAN-COMNET. Our research contributes to the field of social computing by addressing the long-standing challenge of social network generation and opens up new avenues for applications and research that require high-quality social network proxies. In particular, COMNET has been found to be an effective tool for data labeling and enrichment tasks. Additionally, its capability to create synthetic social networks with adapted density has been utilized to analyze the impact of social network topology on machine learning model performance and shed new light on the existing correlation between these two variables. The studies on data labeling, extension, and topological impact are all conducted using Facebook datasets. The corresponding results are presented in two separate papers, which can be accessed through the following links: https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.06566 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.04727. Current state-of-the-art image recognition models rely on convolutional neural networks, which are limited in their ability to explore graph-based relationships within images. In response, we present the Graph Message Transfer Network (GMTN), an artificial neural network designed to tap into these relationships. By projecting image features onto a predefined graph and then iteratively transferring information along its edges, the GMTN is well-suited to capturing interconnected, contextual cues within images. We also introduce the Active GMTN (AGMTN), an enhanced version of the GMTN that dynamically selects the most significant edges to optimize performance. In our tests, the AGMTN outperformed conventional models on a range of tasks, while also reducing the number of required iterations and edges to interact with. As a result, the AGMTN offers a more efficient solution to image recognition problems than standard approaches. We have also made the code for our model public, in accordance with the principles of open-source research. With our model, we successfully replicated the state-of-the-art performance on widely-used benchmark datasets, such as the CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet datasets, among others. Additionally, we have tested the AGMTN on more challenging datasets, such as the ImageNet, and found that it surpassed the performance of state-of-the-art models trained using up-to-date techniques, including those based on deep learning and graph neural networks. In our evaluations, the AGMTN consistently offered a more accurate and efficient solution to image recognition problems than conventional models. We have also performed a detailed analysis of the interior mechanics of our model, in particular how the active edges selection process influences the accuracy of the AGMTN. As a result, the AGMTN represents a more efficient, accurate, and dynamic solution to image recognition problems than conventional models. It is worth noting that the interior mechanics of our model are easily adaptable to a range of scenarios in which it may be beneficial to dynamically select the active edges, extending beyond the simple image recognition tasks that we tested to include tasks like video recognition and graph-based data. Efficient implementation of multiplication circuits is vital for computing systems, particularly ASICs, FPGAs, and ASIPS. This requirement arises from numerous applications across engineering fields that rely heavily on multiplication, such as signal processing and control design. This paper contributes to addressing this need by proposing novel truncated LM(2), LM(3), and LM(4) circuits capable of performing N times a constant with minimal hardware complexity. The proposed LM(2) and LM(3) circuits represent improvements over existing DFM(2) and DFM(3) designs in the literature, with LM(4) circuits outperforming DFM(4) designs for certain scenarios. Moreover, our designed LM(2), LM(3), and multipliers with certain factors can be implemented using less hardware resources than the current best-known Scalable Multiplication Circuit (SMC) designs in the literature, which operate under a distinct multiplication paradigm. The hardware efficiency of these new circuits is demonstrated through various metrics such as hardware area, buffer size, and critical path delay, with comparisons to DFM(2), DFM(3), SMC, and CMUL circuits. The proposed LM(2), LM(3), and multipliers offer significant advantages in terms of hardware complexity while maintaining similar latency characteristics when compared to traditional CML multipliers. The design examples illustrate significant reductions in hardware area, as well as decreased latency and increased throughput for certain applications when using these new circuits over traditional CML designs. The results of our explorations into the hardware parse complexity of these new circuits appear promising, which could potentially facilitate parallelism and thus enhance the overall parsing efficiency. The complete design, including verification files, is made publicly available on GitHub. This work significant contributes to addressing the spanning constant multiplication problem with an efficient multiplication circuit design. Our findings indicate that to explain the observed star properties, the ingested planet had to lose the majority of its angular momentum to the star. This second scenario is similar to the "conserving-angular momentum" model used to explain the star formation in BOSTER. Unlike traditional methods that rely on pre-defined operators, DCAEs learn a unique representation for each image or pixel, allowing for more accurate detection of alterations in urban areas, agricultural landscapes, and other environments. Although successful, using DCAEs has a significant drawback: it consumes vast computational resources and takes a prolonged time to complete, making it impractical for large-scale projects. Moreover, many existing studies fail to address the uncertainty associated with alteration detection, treating all results as absolute facts. The proposed CDCAE method, with its novel unsupervised DCAE features, outperforms existing DCAE techniques in remote sensing applications. We introduce an innovative technique, called two-photon absorption boundary transient-current method (TAPBTCM), which allows for real-time monitoring of three-dimensional charge transport within photo-sensitive materials. In a study using this technique, we examine single-crystalline diamond substrates with various nitrogen-doped concentrations. The TAPBTCM method employs a synchronized laser beam, which scatters into different directions by the Breakdown Event, while we record the Transient Current response triggered by one of these scattered beams. By utilizing fast and highly sensitive data acquisition equipment, we capture the entire current transient as it arises from further charge transport within the diamond substrate. By leveraging the inherent anisotropy of the diamond material, which dictates charge transport direction, we reconstruct a 3D picture of the Breakdown Event's spatial dimensions. This information enables us to derive the diamond substrate's charge carrier mobility. In this research, we report results for substrates containing 1-630 ppm nitrogen doping levels. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the TAPBTCM method's detection limit for mobility is significantly higher ($\sim 10^4$ cm$^2$VnC$^1$S$^1$) compared to conventional techniques, while also allowing for the detection of ultra-low-level infrared illumination. This novel capability stems from the ability of the TAPBTCM method to monitor charge transport across large distances within diamond substrates. In addition, we apply the TAPBTCM method to detect scintillation events resulting from alpha and beta particles as well as X-ray photons. This offers promising possibilities for its future use in particle detector and scintillation detector applications. Lastly, we explore the feasibility and potential limitations of using the TAPBTCM method for detecting coherent acoustic phonons within diamond substrates. These could have significant implications for the field of photothermal measurement science. In summary, the TAPBTCM method is a versatile tool that may be useful for a broad array of research domains, including solid-state physics, particle detection, and biomedicine, as well as photothermal measurement and analysis. By applying the $k_T$ factorization, the incoherent $k_T$-weighted direct photon cross-section can be determined, enabling a comparison with experimental data. Notably, the predicted incoherent $k_T$-weighted direct photon cross-section in Cu$+$Cu collisions at 200 GeV exceeds that of p$+$p collisions at 68 GeV, closely aligning with experimental measurements. The observed agreement between theory and experiment validates the developed coherent direct photon cross-section. Further, the predicted incoherent $k_T$-weighted direct photon cross-section in Au$+$Au collisions at 200 GeV matches experimental findings. Notably, the predicted incoherent $k_T$-weighted direct photon nuclear modification factor $I_{N}$ exhibits positivity in Cu$+$Cu and Au$+$Au collisions at low $p_T$, before transitioning into the $k_T$-filtered 'Baseline' region, where $I_{N}$ becomes $p_{T}$-independent. The observed $I_{N}$ structure, characterized by a rise at low $p_T$ and then becoming $p_{T}$-independent, has been attributed to the 'Baseline' filtering removing $k_T$-correlated direct photons. The use of soft grippers in grasping research is increasing, partly due to their ability to Grasp Various Objects (GVO) capabilities, but they lack the complexity of models that can be used for control purposes. Current models, such as the modified mass-spring-damper model, are simple yet inadequate for predicting the movement of multi-fingered soft grippers. Our work introduces a new approach to modeling and controlling these devices. We have developed a novel virtual modeling method that extracts the system's dynamics from simulated or real trajectories. This method employs the Koopman operator theory, which linearly transforms the system's state space, to identify the forward shift operator. The resulting model can be used to develop predictive controls, such as model predictive control (MPC), for soft grippers. To test our approach, we simulated the movement of a multi-fingered soft gripper in multiple environments, including virtual and real scenarios, and compared its performance to a more traditional PID controller. Our findings show that our model-based MPC controller facilitates more efficient and precise movement of soft grippers in various grasping tasks. Additionally, we demonstrated the applicability of our virtual modeling and regulation method using real-world robotic data from a 3D printing demonstrator. The method has been implemented in a publicly available Python package on GitHub. Experimental studies on the robotic platform have verified the performance of our model and controller. The development of soft grippers for robotic systems has far-reaching applications in 3D printing, where they can be employed for the preparation of composite materials, and have demonstrated high potential in the prepared materials' impact strength. Our work lays the foundation for using the Koopman operator theory in modeling and controlling soft robotic systems. The approach could also be applied to other types of soft robots, such as elliptical robots, and offers a more efficient solution for developing controllers with minimal computational requirements. In the future, we aim to expand the method to accommodate the limitations of soft gripper models that describe their movement using elliptical shapes. Furthermore, we intend to adapt and refine the virtual modeling and regulation method for use with other types of soft robots. Current solutions, such as SGD and Adam, primarily focus on addressing overfitting and acceleration concerns. Our proposed method, OGDC, addresses the slow convergence issue by incorporating a robust bias correction technique. By eliminating the optimization bias, OGDC enables better generalization performance. Importantly, OGDC maintains the acceleration benefits of Adam. Our empirical analysis confirms that OGDC significantly outperforms Adam and other optimizers, particularly in challenging large deep learning scenarios. Further investigation into the role of regularization in optimization reveals that, intriguingly, dropout is already a generalization optimizer. Session-based recommendation systems learn short-term preferences from a user's browser history, but often struggle to offer non-transactional suggestions when no items from previous sessions match. To address this limitation, we've developed an approach that suggests unexplored combinations of products alongside individual items, facilitating discovery of novel product groupings. Our method employs a multi-task transformer architecture, where one task involves modeling item co-occurrence patterns across sessions and another task ranks candidate item combinations based on existing session data. Leveraging two-phase suggestion processing, our system prioritizes relevant individual item suggestions first, followed by the generation of novel product grouping suggestions. This enabling strategy allows users to engage with fresh ideas while reducing the influence of past session exploits. Experimentation on real-world data showcases the benefits of our new grouping suggestion stream, with user studies demonstrating significant gains in suggestion relevance and overall system satisfaction. Additionally, our method outperforms baseline approaches in both objective metrics of suggestion accuracy and system performance. Landmark-based registration is utilized to disseminate information within a swarm of drones, ensuring synchronized navigation and collision avoidance. Our registration method employs a novel centroid-based distance metric that replaces traditional distance calculations, resulting in more accurate and stable alignment, particularly for irregularly shaped point sets. Compared to existing methods, this approach leads to reduced alignment errors and a lower risk of drone collisions. Knowledge from sensors is processed through a decision-based black-box framework, where outputs correspond to quantities of interest through an unknown mapping. Uncertainty quantification in the form of a confidence metric is necessary for post-processing to ensure reliable results. Two approaches for determining confidence are explored, particularly for applications in robotics and autonomous systems: (1) utilizing decision theory and the Brier score as a metric based on prediction intervals, and (2) applying a non-parametric estimate via the calibration gap. Two methods for transferring knowledge from a training set to a real-world environment are also examined: (1) a quantitative approach involving regression analysis to maximize the Brier score, and (2) a qualitative method involving active learning to improve calibration. These techniques are demonstrated to effectively handle cases of non-response and missing data without the need for expensive computational processes. The methods are tested on synthetic and real-world data from an autonomous helicopter system, showing that they yield satisfactory results for reliable decision-making in a diverse range of environments. The proposed methods can be utilized as a pre-processing or post-processing tool to enhance reliability in a wide array of decision-based black-box systems. Random number generation is the foundation for modeling stochastic behavior in various fields, but current methods have significant limitations in terms of speed, precision, and true randomness. To address these issues, this work introduces TuRaN, a novel approach based on extracting random patterns from reduced supply voltage fluctuations in SRAM arrays. TuRaN utilizes a scalable architecture consisting of a column selector, address decoder, and column access module to generate random bits at bitmaster rates of up to 1.6Ts per column (e.g., 2.4GSps at 1.2Ts). This architecture's underlay is designed to achieve the utmost degree of randomness and to easily accommodate large numbers of SRAM columns. Furthermore, TuRaN's full functionality has been demonstrated in a commercial 28nm CMOS process, where the measured random bit error rate did not exceed 0.000103% across various temperatures and voltages. In comparison to established approaches, TuRaN offers superior speed, superior reliability, and the highest degree of randomness. TuRaN is capable of generating up to 64Gbps of random data from a single 1.2V SRAM array, but remains functional even when the power consumption drops to 0.13Ws per bitmaseter. To summarize, TuRaN boasts the highest degree of randomness, the fastest generation rate, the lowest power consumption, the widest operating voltage range, and the longest lifespan compared to other methods. TuRaN's remarkable performance, combined with its compatibility with standard CMOS processes, makes it an ideal solution for stochastic applications in fields such as finance, medical testing, bio-science, geology, military communications, and neural network training. To facilitate widespread adoption, the necessary information to replicate TuRaN has been thoroughly documented and made available online. This includes simulation tools, full design files, and experimental results demonstrating TuRaN's reliability and performance across various process nodes and temperatures. To address any potential concerns regarding intellectual property, TuRaN's patent applications have been filed and are currently under review. This work is expected to have a significant impact in various fields, where stochastic behavior is present, and will likely lead to the widespread adoption of TuRaN as a genuine random number generator. In the context of decentralized machine learning, we investigate an federal learning setting where a central node desires to distribute a robust model to peripheral nodes via a communication-efficient training process. To this end, we enhance the standard Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD) algorithm by introducing Distributional Robust Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DR-DSGD). DR-DSGD optimizes a weighted sum of empirical risks from the local datasets, with each node weighted equally and potentially different, subject to a constraint on total weight 1 together with an empirical graph topology constraint. via careful analysis under data label noise and non-symmetric datashifting between nodes, we establish DR-DSGD's convergence rate over a regularized empirical risk minimization solution and demonstrate substantial communication efficiency improvements over DSGD, specifically a logarithmic improvement in convergence rate per iteration. Our analysis also holds under general connected graph topologies and in the presence of fading gradient noise. We test DR-DSGD in a control application and find that it performs better than DSGD, particularly in scenarios with significant data shifting between nodes. DR-DSGD also exhibits logarithmic convergence and demonstrates a 2-3 iteration convergence rate improvement compared to DSGD in various noisy conditions. DR-DSGD is now publicly available on GitHub.

Research indicates that an extreme state of matter, often referred to as a Quark-Gluon Plasma (QGP), exists within these collisions, but the process by which the QGP converts into a more stable state still lacks clarification. In this study, we examine the radial and non-radial flow components within these collisions, their respective contributions to overall particle production, and how they are influenced by varying initial nuclear states. Our analysis reveals that, in peripheral collisions, the radial flow component dominates particle production, whereas non-radial flow plays a more significant role in less peripheral collisions. Moreover, the number of charged particles generated through hydrodynamic pullers exceeds that of radial flow alone, particularly noticeable in the most central collisions. This complements previous studies by Speranza et al. and Gyulines et al., which also observed an enhanced yield of charged particles in central collisions. In the field of cancer research, multiple sample collections from a single patient are analyzed across various subsets of genes to gauge treatment impact. This approach, known as the basket trial, offers a compassionate alternative for measuring gene mutations' effect on patient outcomes. Statistical analysis in these trials typically focuses on evaluating the relationship between treatment groups and outcome measures, such as progression-free survival or response rates. New approaches are being developed to enhance accuracy by assessing the magnitude of treatment effects in sub-groups. Our method utilizes Bayesian statistics to determine the magnitude of treatment effects in basket trials that analyze multiple samples from a single patient. Our approach borrows information between sub-groups by incorporating shared prior uncertainty. This novel method addresses the sparsity issue encountered in single-patient trials, providing more precise estimates than traditional methods. Results from simulated data indicate improved performance over frequentist methods and our approach outperforms existing ones. This article will feature a mathematical framework for the Bayesian magnitude assessment, results from simulated data, and comparisons with established methods. Additionally, application examples from the SARMM-CL100 basket trial complementing our mathematical framework with real-world data are presented. Our approach can handle various types of outcome measures and will be made available as an open-source R package. Motion systems that experience variations in their dynamics can be addressed by sequential loop closing, which involves making local linear parameter varying models more accurate by incorporating systemic parameters that affect the motion's dynamics. By incorporating these parameters in a sequential manner, rather than all at once, sequential loop closing enables motion control designers to refine their design with greater precision. This work examines the effects of sequential loop closing on high-accuracy motion systems, specifically a flyby spacecraft's antenna motion controller, and finds that the method can significantly boost positional error residuals. Notably, the research reveals that while initial sequential closing steps yield improved performance, later steps may introduce stability issues in the closed-loop system, prompting the proposal of a novel stability assessment technique. This study also compares three different systemic parameter estimation methods and evaluates their impact on sequential closing. Ultimately, the research indicates that sequential closing offers a valuable approach for enhancing high-accuracy motion control performance, but developers must carefully consider the impacts of successive system identifications on stability. This study presents the results of a simulated test in space, which is also replicated in a laboratory setting using an actuated antenna-on-fly platform. The research demonstrates that sequential closing can significantly improve motion tracking performance, but warns against over-iteration that may compromise system stability. This work aims to contribute to research on linear parameter varying systems and sequential closing, while addressing the critical issue of stability in motion control design. This 'collider metric' evaluates potential instability discovery capabilities in both proton-proton and electron-positron colliders, taking into consideration various production processes and decay modes. Our analysis reveals that a 100~TeV proton collider offers the greatest advantage for detecting the SM instability through heavy particle production, whereas a linear electron collider is more capable of pinpointing the instability through direct direct loops. Additionally, our study demonstrates that a 100~km or 200~km energy-recovering electron collider can significantly outperform the 100~TeV proton collider in identifying the SM instability through the $Z$-boson loop at electron-positron collisions. A corresponding 'detector metric' evaluates the efficiency of different detector designs in identifying the SM instability, with the optimal detector featuring a highly advanced electroweak precision detector capability. This research also introduces an innovative approach to searching for the SM instability at lower energy colliders, revealing that the LHC, SHC (300 TeV), and FCC-c (100 TeV) have the potential to pinpoint the instability through specific production processes at corresponding energy scales of 34, 65, and 100 TeV. A novel approach called Cycle-Partitioning GAN is introduced, which uses a deep learning strategy called Deepmind's Cyclic Self-Supervision, in conjunction with a novel instance division method called Unmarked Instance Division, to tackle the issue of data heterogeneity within domains. The Cycle-Partitioning GAN employs an unsupervised data division method that splits data into multiple cycles, and then connects them in a cycle-to-cycle manner through a generator and an encoder. By doing so, it minimizes the disparity between these cycles through a discriminator that assesses the partitioned data's coherence. In contrast to existing methods, the Cycle-Partitioning GAN performs instance division at an individual level, in addition to cycle-level division. As a result, it facilitates the training of a single model across diverse data configurations without the need for data parallelism or pre-trained knowledge distillation. The effectiveness of the Cycle-Partitioning GAN is demonstrated through its application on three real-world image datasets, in particular, EuC2v, EuC4v, and 3D Burdett, all of which have unlabeled modalities that vary progressively. Consequently, it shows considerable potential in handling data configuration issues that may arise in various applications and scenarios. The code for the Cycle-Partitioning GAN is available on GitHub at the repository address provided. Experiments and the model's architecture will be discussed in further detail below. TPC enhances the normal distribution of point clouds and preserves the intrinsic geometry and topological structures of the original point cloud through a multi-scale feature extraction module. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of TPC in maintaining the original point cloud's geometry and topological structures, as well as its superiority over existing methods in preserving the domain-specific geometry and topological structures of global and local down-sampling operations. Additionally, a wide range of applications have shown that geometric and topological structures are vital components of point clouds. The code for TPC is available on GitHub at https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/main/tensorflow/python/eager/tpc.py.

We're investigating medium access techniques in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks, looking at Slotted ALOHA and CSMA to eliminate the collisions that occur when multiple radars use the same frequency at the same time. Our solution, a modified CSMA algorithm, works by having each radar wait for a set time until it transmits, based on the time it takes for the radar's signal to reach a distant target and return back. This "interframe period" is calculated using the radar's distance, which changes slowly, so CSMA works well in these radar networks. Our results show that CSMA significantly reduces collisions compared to ALOHA, and we test these algorithms on a 2D graph to visualize their performance. Our code is available online for others to use. We evaluated our algorithms using the following metrics: the average number of active radars that transmit at the same time (collisions), the average number of active radars that transmit at the same time per unit of time (collateral transmissions), the percentage of radars that experience collisions, the time between collisions (interarrival time), the number of radars that experience collisions per unit of time (utilization), the network's capacity (defined as the number of radars that can use the same frequency without collisions, or "safety factor"), the average number of active radars that transmit at the same time per unit of time in a small area of the network (local utilization), the average number of active radars that transmit at the same time per unit of time that are a certain distance away from each other (neighborliness), the number of radlers in the network that experience collisions because of another radar's transmissions (network's "noise"). Our results show that CSMA significantly outperforms ALOHA in reducing collisions and improving performance. Our research also provides insights for future studies on medium access techniques in FMCW radar networks. Our solution also provides a tool for evaluating the performance of radar networks. The EPR paradox's core problem, according to Einstein, Podolski, and Rosen, lay in the instantaneous correlation of particles' properties, particularly position and momentum, which they saw as violating the principle of locality. Their considerations, however, were limited to ideal measurements and scenarios where the Born rule applies uniformly. In reality, measurements with distinct outcomes and probabilities not dictated by the Born rule do occur in such scenarios. Our work demonstrates, using a specific example of double-slit interference, that the essence of Bell nonlocality can be observed in the quantity of instantaneous correlation, which is evident in the coexistence of nonzero momentum and position probabilities for a single particle. Importantly, Bell's theorem can be seen as a consequence of assumptions about the completeness of measurements and correlation properties, which are challenged by our findings. Our results indicate that Bell nonlocality can be expressed simply as the condition for existing in potentially conflicting momentum and position eigenstates together. Consequently, Bell nonlocality arises naturally from the inherent properties of quantum states, rendering unnecessary the comparison of different sets of measurement outcomes in different laboratories. Our approach thereby offers a straightforward, inequality-free illustration of Bell nonlocality, which we hope will prove useful in clarifying the underlying principles of quantum mechanics for students and anyone who may have found traditional explanations confounding. Ultimately, we believe that Bell nonlocality, rather than being a mere theoretical artifact, holds significant potential as a fundamental property of nature. Our work also addresses a long-outstanding question in the literature by showing that quantum states' non-orthogonal purity, which is often seen as a local property, in fact necessitates the violation of Bell's inequality. In addition, we have established a critical distinction between classical states, which we define as having zero cross-sections between distinct outcomes, and quantum states, which are distinguished not only by nonzero cross-sections but also by Bell nonlocality. Our approach to illustrating Bell nonlocality has the added benefit of highlighting a previously underappreciated aspect of quantum mechanics, which we believe will prove valuable in future educational and theoretical endeavors. Our method also enables the examination of quantum mechanics within continuous-dimensional spaces and their relationships to special cases in discrete-dimensional spaces. Our approach to illustrating Bell nonlocality has been formally checked for accuracy using mathematical methods. Our results have further revealed a previously unappreciated link between Bell nonlocality and the condition for states to be distinguishable in momentum and position, which we believe will prove valuable in future educational and theoretical endeavors. It explores the limitations of traditional safety-critical systems and introduces fail-functional concepts. The SSREF model is utilized to develop a fail-functional driving system contingency plan. The paper also describes the methods used to analyze and demonstrate the effectiveness of this plan, focusing on its ability to prevent and mitigate system failures. Unlike conventional safety systems, which aim to prevent hazards, fail-functional systems aim to minimize their impact. The analysis of the contingency plan within the SSREF framework reveals that it adheres to three fundamental principles: it's failure-preventing, minimally failure-indicative, and failure-correcting. The paper ultimately concludes by highlighting that the contingency plan's success hinges on its ability to minimize and correct failures, and that this approach should be considered for future automotive fail-functional system designs. Identifying clusters in complex systems like power grids, internet networks, and climate patterns is crucial for proper operation, security, and policy planning. Current methods for identifying clusters in these systems, such as eigenvalue-based approaches, often rely on predefined or estimated parameters that may not accurately represent the systems' behavior. Additionally, these methods can only suggest potential clusters, but may miss existing ones or identify unnecessary ones. Furthermore, these methods can be computationally expensive and are only feasible for small systems. We introduce a novel method that uses time-series data to identify clusters in dynamical systems while minimizing the number of parameters needed. This approach uses the systems' underlying network topology to organize the data into meaningful groups. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method on various networks, such as the California power grid, a climate pattern network, and a network of connected oscillators, outperforming traditional methods in accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency. This method can be scalable for large systems and provides valuable insights into the systems' structure. We make our code available for reproducing the results at https://github.com/epss-ku/IBC. One key limitation of existing hybrid recommender systems lies in their reliance on predetermined side information, neglecting the influential document context and ignoring the dynamic interplay between such information in preference formation. To address this, we present a pioneering hybrid framework that integrates an collaborative filtering method with two contextual relevance models, thereby capturing the intrinsic value of side information and contextual factors. Furthermore, this system adapts to changing user preferences and context by learning to aggregate information and filter out noisy signals. Evaluation on real-world datasets reveals the superiority of our approach over comparative systems in terms of accuracy and fairness, demonstrating its potential to yield improved outcomes in recommender systems. To showcase the efficacy of this system in practical scenarios, two case studies are also conducted. One examines its capacity to learn context-aware item representations, whereas the other highlights its ability to mitigate the bias inherent in side information. In essence, this system contributes to the development of more comprehensive and strategic methods of information aggregation in hybrid recommender systems. Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted ranking systems, with a particular advantage when combined with ranking models. Nonetheless, applying these pre-trained models is labor-intensive due to the time and effort required to label data. To address this challenge, research has been conducted on methods to efficiently utilize pre-trained models via knowledge distillation. In this study, we present a novel approach called PILE that leverages multiple teachers to improve ranking performance while being computationally efficient. PILE operates by iterating through logit collection from multiple teachers and aggregating these logits to create new labels for self-supervised learning. This process enables multiple teachers to contribute equally and prevents imbalance in the ranking pipeline. Through theoretical analysis and experiments on real-world datasets, the effectiveness of PILE is demonstrated, particularly on CTN-based ranking models, where it outperforms current state-of-the-art knowledge distillation methods by a significant margin. To significantly improve this issue, we introduce a novel history term, enabling the completion of the associated semi-discrete system to a variety of higher-order continuous systems. Both methods are theoretically validated and supported by numerical experiments showcasing their effectiveness. Crucially, the numerical results illustrate that the completed systems can be interpreted as being the product of two higher-order approximations - one in space and one in time - when the transport velocity is sufficiently smooth. The growth in distributed ML training via federated learning is driven by concerns for users' data confidentiality and control over their data. However, questions remain over the intersection of FL's goals of inclusivity, fairness, and privacy, particularly in contrast to existing techniques. This work delves into the implications of FL for sensitive user groups and proposes a novel DP framework, known as Differential Federated Learning (DFL), which reconciles ML's accuracy needs with equitable outcomes and strict data protection requirements. Two key scenarios in DFL involve horizontal partitioning and vertical partitioning, with the latter offering a more general solution with the integration of DP. This integration allows for a novel interpretation of fairness metrics, such as the relationship between equity and privacy, which was previously unexplored. This leads to several key findings: firstly, under certain conditions, integrations of equity and privacy standards are achievable; secondly, when user data shares the same structure, perfect equity can coexist with up to $\log_2(N)$ bits of privacy for large $N$; and thirdly, when considering vertical federations with more than two participants, achieving perfect equity necessitates the use of more than two bits of privacy. Two key lessons can be learned here: firstly, the integration of equity and privacy standards in FL is more restrictive than what was previously thought possible; and, secondly, the concepts of equity and privacy are interdependent in the context of FL, with certain standards of equity limiting the amount of privacy that can be achieved. This work offers the first accreditation of empirical ML training as DP, thereby marking a significant advancement towards achieving equity and privacy-friendly FL training. Two such training methods, known as DP-Federated Averaging and DP-Cyclic Averaging, were developed and demonstrated to be accurate and robust, even in complex, non-symmetrical scenarios, such as neural network training for image classification tasks. Two key lessons can also be learned here: firstly, the integration of DP and equity standards in FL training methods, such as DP-Federated Averaging, can achieve results that are almost as accurate to those of the dominant FL training methods; and, secondly, these new training methods, such as DP-Cyclic Averaging, offer improved performance and robustness over existing FL training methods, particularly those based on empirical averaging. Under a budget constraint for communication, we demonstrate that model-parallel approaches can be optimized through a review process that is both efficient in terms of bits and dependent on the data. We then introduce a region-based training method that is capable of handling complex models on local datasets with multiple devices, with each device containing data from the original dataset. We test this approach on a variety of use cases, including learning Gaussian Basis functions and RBF networks with up to 500 components, demonstrating its effectiveness under various communication limitations. Additionally, we show that region-based training outperforms model averaging and remote training methods in terms of reconstruction error and training time. Our proposed method remains accurate, with a minimal decrease in performance even under the most restrictive communication conditions. To validate its efficacy, we present a region-based training protocol that is compatible with existing deep learning frameworks, with an accompanying codebase available on GitHub. We evaluate our approach on several image classification tasks, showcasing its ability to provide accurate models under various communication scenarios. Our results indicate that region-based training offers the best possible outcome under restricted communication conditions, with a minimal decrease in performance even after multiple iterations. This approach provides a general solution for distributed training of deep neural networks, with applications in mobile edge computing and local distribution of AI models. A common issue in machine learning is achieving good performance both in optimization and generalization. Some methods aim to enhance model capabilities, while others focus on modifying optimization techniques; yet, few have explored the vast potential of programmatic feature engineering. This study introduces a general, versatile approach to creating new features from the existing ones, based on the idea of iterating and combining different transformations. Importantly, our method is transparent, allowing for extensive analysis and feature selection. When applied to the task of optimizing LSTM network performance on the IMDB and AgNews datasets, our method leads to significant generalization performance gains and enables efficient optimization. Additionally, our method facilitates the extraction of rich, high-order features from the original data features. Notably, our features and the corresponding analysis shed light on the long-standing question of whether improved generalization performance necessarily corresponds to deeper models. To overcome these challenges, this paper introduces a novel iterative approach based on the iterative closest point (ICP) algorithm, which allows for simultaneous generation of multiple complex structures in 3D volumetric tissue. The proposed method first applies ICP to determine the optimal sample position, and then utilizes this information to design a focused focal plane for each target structure. Building upon this, a binary lens array is calculated based on the previously obtained focal points. The iteration process continues until convergence is achieved. The method's effectiveness is validated through experiments involving two examples: generating two fluorescent dyes in 4D hydrogel and creating two optical triggers for stem cell activation in 3D hydrogel. The results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm enables the simultaneous generation of multiple complex structures in 3D volumetric tissue with high precision and a wide range of focal lengths. The associated system demonstrates high flexibility, as evidenced by successful patterning of multiple structures with various sizes and a deep axial modulation. The technique has the potential for widespread use in biology and medicine due to its ease of use, fast processing times, and adaptability for controlling cells and living organisms. The developed system, as presented in this study, showcases an unprecedented degree of complexity and depth, as well as a substantial array size of 256x256 elements. The findings further reveal that the method can be optimized further to accommodate an even larger array size of 256x256 elements. However, these sensors have limited functionality due to the slow multiplication rate. To overcome this, researchers have proposed the small collection-electrode technology demonstrator (CLICTD), which incorporates active quenching and signal amplification, in combination with a highly sensitive single-photon detection system. This concept has been demonstrated in CMOS technology developed in 2015-2016. In this study, CLICTD's performance has been evaluated using different sensor thicknesses and substrates, tailored to be compatible with the CLIC detector research. Experimental data and simulation results are presented to investigate the sensor's time-use efficiency, active region length, hit output, and signal-to-noise ratio. Analysis of the CLICTD's performance in a 25 $\mu$m thick sensor designed for mono-crystalline silicon and poly-crystalline silicon substrates reveals a high level of compatibility with the CLIC detector's specifications. Our research presents a groundbreaking approach called Rapid Atmospheric Self-coherent Imaging, which employs sophisticated signal processing techniques to harness the inherent coherency in atmospheric turbulence and directly capture speckles on telescopes without needing sophisticated wavefront sensors. Recent breakthroughs in this method's computer simulations and theoretical frameworks have paved the way for successful laboratory tests, which we outline in this study. These trials involved the successful regulation of speckle velocities on a telescope simulator at the Santa Cruz Adaptive Optics Testbed, resulting in speaker images with speckle sizes as small as 40 micro-radiants at 160 Hz. Our findings indicate that this method can effectively mitigate the performance limitations of current AO systems, particularly for high spatial bandlimited systems. While still in its early stages, this technology holds considerable promise for future ground-based astronomical observations and devices. Nonetheless, significant enhancements to the speaker's hardware and our signal processing algorithms are necessary to achieve this vision, and we outline our plan for subsequent research milestones to achieve this goal. Our ultimate goal is to achieve speckle sizes of as small as 10 micro-radiants at 160 Hz, which is a crucial requirement for maximizing the speaker's potential resolution, and we anticipate making substantial progress in the upcoming years. Moreover, our follow-up research will focus on linear system theory and performance predictions for the speaker, and we expect to demonstrate a speaker resolution of around 20 milli-arcseconds with an integration time of around 1 millisecond. This represents a speaker resolution that approaches the speaker's Nyquist sampling limit, and our follow-up research will focus on developing a speaker architecture and signal processing algorithms that can effectively realize this performance. Our ultimate aim is to achieve a speaker resolution of around 0.5 milli-arcseconds with an integration time of around 1 millisecond, which is a speaker resolution that surpasses current AO systems by around 10 times the speaker resolution of the KDAO system on the Keck Deimos instrument. In particular, we find that a 10-year run of DUNE, equipped with its planned two modules, could provide evidence of sterile neutrinos in certain configurations at a 95% confidence level, particularly in regions with low densities and long-range distances like neutrino beams from SPS or LBNL. This study introduces an advanced simulation method that enables more accurate modeling of particle collisions in fluidized beds by incorporating multiple time steps. Typically, existing simulation algorithms utilize a single time step for each particle collision, leading to artificially lengthened collision durations that vary depending on the simulation's spatial resolution. This can result in unrealistic collision times of several microseconds, as observed in a recent study. To address this issue, our proposed method utilizes two distinct time steps - a primary step for the main fluid dynamics simulation, and a secondary step specifically designed to model the complex and prolonged processes involved in particle collisions. By implementing a multi-time-step algorithm, we are able to simulate collision processes lasting up to 100 microseconds, as seen in a test simulation of a colliding pair of particles. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that the proposed method significantly reduces collision-related deviations, as shown in a 3D particle collision simulation involving 102 particles. These advancements enable more precise modeling of particle collisions, facilitating more accurate simulations of fluidized beds. As a result, our method opens up new possibilities for simulating various phenomena associated with extended particle collisions, including prolonged contact times and multiple collision sequences. To verify the efficacy of our approach, we conducted a series of tests, including a demonstration of a particle collision resulting in a permanent particle deformation. These validation tests confirm that the proposed method can accurately model the collision process, as seen in a comparison between simulated and real-world images of a colliding particle. Finally, our study involves a simulation of a complex 3D domain containing 102 particles, as shown in a visual depiction, and demonstrates the potential for widespread applications of our method in modeling various particle-based systems. Based on these findings, we conclude that our multi-time-step algorithm presents a valuable and efficient solution for accurately simulating particle collisions. As a result, our method is expected to significantly contribute to the development of more precise and longer-scale particle-based simulations, as shown in a comparison with existing collision models. Furthermore, our research reveals that the primary step frequency should be aligned with the fluid dynamics time scale, and the secondary step frequency should be based on the particle size, as seen in a test simulation of a particle pair. These findings present new and interesting research avenues, as well as potential future developments in this field. We go on to identify additional constraints on $k$ and $n$ and, by considering the difference between $a$ and $b$ as $2d$, derive necessary conditions for $2k+1$ and $d$. Mordell, is similar to the approach taken by K. Harborth in 1977, and extends the findings of N. Arnold, B. Dietz, and K. Harborth as reported in 1991. The data were recorded at a center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV and an integrated luminosity of 12.3 $\mu$b$^{-1}$. The study covers a rapidity range of 2.5 and 3.0 and transverse momentum up to 35 GeV/$c$ for J/$\psi$ and 20 GeV/$c$ for $\psi$(2S). The findings show that there is a decrease in the production of J/$\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) as the transverse momentum increases, more noticeable in the middle and highest collision energies. The study found that there is a 60$\pm$7% suppression of J/$\psi$ and a 70$\pm$14% suppression of $\psi$(2S) at 8-12 GeV/$c$ in the most central collisions. The study also discovered that there is a decrease in the $R_{AA}$ of J/$\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) as the transverse momentum increases, more pronounced in $\psi$(2S). The study further notes that the suppression of J/$\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) as the transverse momentum increases is more noticeable in the 8-12 GeV/$c$ range than in the 2-5 GeV/$c$ range. The study found that the suppression of J/$\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) as the transverse momentum increases follows a similar trend in the Large System Radial Flow Model. The study also discovered that the suppression of $\psi$(2S) is due to suppression of prompt and nonprompt $\psi$(2S) mesons. The study found that suppression of prompt $\psi$(2S) mesons follows the trend predicted by the Next-to-Leading-Order Nuclear Factor model. The study further notes that the suppression of nonprompt $\psi$(2S) mesons follows the trend predicted by the Prompt and Non-Prompt Model. The study also discovered that the ratio of J/$\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) as the transverse momentum increases remains constant in the most central collisions but decreases in the semi-central collisions. The study further notes that the study found no dependence on rapidity or collision energy.

In this study, we discuss various formulations of the problem that have been addressed by other mathematicians and present new results for each of these variants. The latter part of the article focuses on a particular formulation given by Allen, Friedlander, and Rusek and shows that $n$ can be as low as $43$ to satisfy the given condition. In this case, we prove that $n$ can be as low as $23$. The article addresses yet another scenario where the given integers are distinct, but may also repeat within the set $\{a_1, \ldots, a_n\}$. The adiabatic index $\Gamma$ represents a fundamental characteristic of dense matter, influencing the endpoint of neutron star mergers and core-collapse supernovae. In this study, we synthesize various calculations of nuclear, neutron star, and liquid metal crusts to construct a comprehensive adiabatic index $\Gamma$ profile for dense matter as a function of density and temperature. Our integrated model covers five distinct density regimes: high-density neutron star matter, dense nuclear matter formed in the core of neutron stars and heavy compact objects, and the liquid metal core with its associated thermal bath. Our $\Gamma$ profile enables predictions about thermal expansions in different density regimes, with notable variations expected. Furthermore, we analyze how $\Gamma$ changes with temperature in various systems, which has implications for the thermal radiative emission of neutron stars. Our integrated model allows the thermal expansion and radiative emission of neutron stars to be predicted based on their masses, enabling the reconstruction of $\Gamma$ from observational data of compact stars. Our integrated model also facilitates the comparison of thermal properties with and without strangeness in the core of neutron stars and other objects, such as kaonless and kaon-fragmentation compact stars. Our analysis indicates that the presence of strange quark cores causes thermal expansion to transition from solid to liquid or solid with liquid droplets as temperature increases, whereas solid cores due to neutron-proton interactions or in neutron star merges do not exhibit this behavior. Our understanding of adiabatic index $\Gamma$ and thermal expansion, with and without strangeness, is expected to contribute to the analysis of future multimessenger datasets of neutron star mergers and other compact objects. Our integrated model also enables the investigation of other phenomena, such as the behavior of neutron star crusts in X-ray transients and the thermal emission of isolated neutron stars and white dwarfs. Our integrated model is based on the public available code NS Mayer's Table Generator, which we updated to construct the necessary tables for our analysis. This updated generator, incorporating our new $\Gamma$ profile, is available at [http://nmstmg.web.uni-freiburg.de/]. Our new $\Gamma$ profile is also available at [https://www.physik.uni-freiburg.de/npnsm/tables.html]. In our accompanying paper, we present the updated table generator and the new $\Gamma$ profile in detail. This work was partially motivated by the NS Physics Working Group's report on neutron star physics, which we contributed to. This research received support from Shinshu
