In protoplanetary disks, carbon monoxide (CO) depleteness may be influenced by various factors such as chemical reactions, ice formation, and dynamic processes like the formation of a mass transition disk. Our study aims to distinguish between these factors in the AS 209 disk, using the Molecules with ALMA at Planet-creating Scales (MAPS) survey. This survey employs ALMA band 7 and 5 data to analyze CO 2-1 and 3-2 lines, along with HCO+ 1-0 and CI 1-0 lines. To assess CO's physical and chemical conditions, we analyze optical depth, H2 column density, and gas temperature. We compare these parameters with model predictions from the one-dimensional gas evolution model 'PRODIM'. Our analysis reveals a double-peaked CO distribution and a CI distribution with a single peak at larger radii. This CI distribution appears as a low-density gas layer extending from ~30 to 100 AU. CI's 3-2 line shows a higher optical depth than expected in solid particles, indicating that this species is primarily present in the gas phase within this radius range. However, CI's 1-0 line exhibits a contrary behavior, displaying a lower optical density than expected from gas-phase CI. This implies that this CI is primarily in solid particles. We observe a CO 'gap' that aligns with the inner disk's 1.3 temperature transition disk boundary, yet CO's 2-1 line shows a double-peaked distribution only at lower temperatures (~15 K). This peak CO distribution at lower temperatures is thought to be from gas that has been chemically altered. Our results suggest the possibility of a gas reduction or chemical processing CO 'gap' in this protoplanetary disk. Moreover, this CO 'gap' appears less distinct by looking only at CO's 2-1 line data. CI's inner disk distribution also suggests a reduction in gas-disk density, possibly resulting from CI's incorporation into solids by the effects of photochemistry and chemical processing. Ultimately, this reduction in gas-disk density may contribute to the formation of massive planets in this system. For AS 209, the gas reduction or chemical processing of CO is more apparent than dynamic processes like the 'transition disk' alone. MAPS's data allow for a more in-depth understanding of carbon's complex formation and evolution processes in protoplanetary disks. Recent studies using Gaia DR2 data have introduced the concept of "stellar threads" - apparently disconnected particles of stars in the galaxy's velocity distribution. We re-explore this idea using more accurate data from Gaia DR5 and early version of Gaia Benchmark stars release 1.1. By utilizing the LoSThreadFinder algorithm, 506,823 stellar components were identified in the Milky Way's bulge and bar areas. However, only 0.033% of these components consist of more than three stars. Furthermore, features consisting of multiple Gaia sources that merely pass a velocity-based filter, without meeting the criterion of seamless space distribution, are found to be unrepresentative of the galaxy's structure, largely consisting of triples and higher-stage stars in random spatial arrangement. Moreover, when evaluating the velocity dispersion of these "stellar threads" in the bulge and bar areas, we noticed a notable increase in velocity dispersion for components consisting of multiple Gaia sources compared to features formed by a single Gaia source, which shows a notable difference ($\sim 10-50\,\mbox{km s}^{-1}$), suggesting a misclassification of distant triple systems as galactic "threads". In contrast to the notion that these "stellar threads" are primarily horizontal in the galaxy, we found 46% of the components with sufficient parallax data exhibit a significant vertical aspect, with many of these featuring relatively narrow height distributions ($\sim 0.2^{\mcirc}$). When evaluating the distribution of these "stellar threads" in the galaxy, we found 58% of the components have right ascension dispersion ($\sigma_{\varphi}$) greater than or equal to $5^{\circ}$, which is essentially random and contradicts the notion of elongated structures in the galaxy's north-south direction. In contrast, we discovered that rich star clusters in the areas we studied do indeed possess distinct, elongated shapes. Our study reveals that these "stellar threads" are essentially just Gaia-resolved star clusters waiting to be dissected into their core structure, with the number of these structures expected to decrease as spatial information becomes available. Furthermore, we found "stellar threads" are predominantly found in areas with high star density, particularly in areas that are hard to disengage into distinct structures in the galaxy's velocity distribution. However, current techniques requiring devices to keep their models and gradient buffers in sync lead to underutilized devices and delayed completion. Existing solutions, involving devices synchronizing with the central server and delaying local updates on the server, compromise efficiency. This paper explores alternatives, enabling devices to execute updates independently and sending accumulated gradients from devices to the server when ready. Yet, since gradient buffers on devices may contain outdated information, the server may perform duplicate computations. Evaluation with Google Drive data also reveals that the proposed methods excel in diverse network conditions. Lastly, this study provides in-depth analysis of the proposed approaches, addressing concerns of efficiency, reliability, and scalability, and identifies areas for further research. To enhance the robustness of visual navigation systems powered by deep reinforcement learning, it is crucial to regulate the learning process to prevent data overfitting. Existing methods controlling deep model training typically focus on maintaining representation disentanglement or preventing feature repetition. Unlike previous techniques that aim to restrict data utilization, we introduce a novel strategy where the learning process is guided by the principle of maximizing representation uncertainty or keeping representation novelty as high as possible. By employing theoretical insights into the relationship between representation entropy and novelty, we present a unified deep reinforcement learning framework for multi-task visual navigation that can automatically detect novel features in each environment and incentivize agents to explore them. Experimental evaluations conducted in multiple benchmark scenarios, such as benchmark datasets and real-world robots, demonstrate that the introduced method outperforms state-of-the-art visual navigation models in terms of success rate in novel environments. Specifically, it achieves a 14.8% higher success rate in novel scenarios compared to the baseline method while also reducing overfitting by 87.3%. The implemented method is now available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/kohli-siddharth/Visual-Navigation-with-Novelty. We offer an alternative, geometry-independent explanation for the occurrence of isolated Dirac bands in 2D systems containing random, non-locally coupled disorders. By developing an analytical approach based on the self-consistent Born approximation, we generate a set of detailed, detailed, spatially-averaged rules that describe the precise placement of isolated Dirac bands in partial topological insulators. According to our findings, the placement of these bands is solely influenced by an island-like property that can be measured using our newly developed $Q$-factor metric. A key operational concern in human-robot collaboration is ensuring that humans and robots can efficiently work together in the same physical space. The collaboration's effectiveness depends on an optimal alignment of their operational spaces to minimize disruptions and errors. While aligning the spaces may involve positional and directional discrepancies, simply closing the position gap gap may lead to large directional errors, resulting in poor performance and potentially even accidents. To address this issue, we introduce a new method that employs the concept of parallel transport to align the operational spaces of humans and robots during tasks like assembling and placing objects. Our approach recognizes the underlying structural information in point clouds to model the surfaces of objects and their corresponding operational spaces. The proposed method then uses the surface information to estimate the optimal alignment target for the end-effector based on the shortest path with minimal directional disruptions. Additionally, our technique extends the classic Iterative Closest Point algorithm to handle the adaptation challenges by effectively coping with gaps in the data and efficient handling of large directional discrepancies. Through simulations and real-world experiments, we demonstrate the proposed method's ability to achieve significant performance gains, with improved results when compared to current human-robot collaboration techniques. Specifically, we achieved a 3.30 times speed boost and reduced the number of iteration steps by a factor of 2.34, while also demonstrating robustness and efficient convergence. The developed method is now available as part of the ROS ecosystem, enabling its immediate application in a wide range of human-robot collaboration scenarios. Further research will focus on adapting the underlying surfaces to facilitate more general human-robot collaboration scenarios. Although advanced computer visions can efficiently detect motion from visual data, transferring this information to physical properties in 3D space remains a significant obstacle due to the complexity of such translations. In real-life situations, precise measurements of rotational velocities are rarely captured; instead, velocities are often expressed in terms of unexpected rotations (e.g., "the ball spun around quickly"). In this research, we explore how to utilize observed rotations in unexpected situations to determine the 3D positions of objects, introducing the Unintentional Turntable Problem to achieve this goal. Convolutional Networks are highly successful in image classification tasks, but they treat the orientation of edges in images as irrelevant. In contrast, various studies across computer vision and graphics have demonstrated the importance of edge orientation. This paper introduces a novel type of Convolutional Network called Orientation Convolutive Networks, where each filter consists of multiple sub-filters aligned at different angles, and all sub-filters share the same weight. This model leverages the interactions between sub-filters to capture essential features and significantly reduces the parameter count. By optimizing the angular distribution of filters, the model achieves better representation than conventional Convolutional Networks. Experimental results on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 demonstrate that Orientation Convolutive Networks outperform basic Convolutional Networks, and they also perform competitively on ResNet-18 and MobileNetV2. This model's source code is available online. The experiments confirm that the model's performance benefits from training it on GAN-distributed data. Additionally, the model's parameters scale similarly to MobileNetV2, but it exhibits a substantial performance gap. This study delves into the model's inner workings and the effects of training methods. Furthermore, the model is tested on ImageNet, and the associated code is available at https://github.com/IndigoPurple/OrientationConvolutiveNetworks. The model's performance is superior to the state-of-the-art Lightweight MobileNetV2 variations. This study's contributions are three-fold. First, a novel model called Orientation Convolutive Networks is introduced. Second, it is demonstrated that the model's performance benefits from training it on GAN-distributed data. Third, the model's parameters are as sparse as Half-MobileNetV2, yet it outperforms it by a significant margin. Ultimately, this study is inspired by the observation that the model's performance benefits from training it on GAN-distributed data, and it is hypothesized that this phenomenon may also occur in other Convolutional Network architectures. Therefore, it is suggested that GAN-distributed data may hold the key to achieving exceptional performance with minimal parameter requirements. Recent advancements in deep learning technologies have led to the breakthroughs in distributed training for neural networks, enabling the training of robust neural networks resistant to manipulation and data corruption. Despite this, a new threat has emerged in the form of neural Trojan attacks, which clandestine agents can employ to secretly manipulate Neural Network behavior. Existing countermeasures against these attacks have primarily concentrated on recognizing and mitigating malicious embeddings within the Neural Network itself. Nevertheless, as Neural Networks become increasingly utilized in safety-sensitive applications such as healthcare and finance, there is a growing need to protect them from being compromised by Trojan attacks. In this paper, we introduce SHTA - Semantic Hostless Trojan Assault, the first-ever hostless backdoor attack that can be executed remotely. We also develop an effective countermeasure to protect Neural Networks from SHTA. Our research provides a fundamental understanding of the newly identified threat known as SHTA and serves as a framework for future research in this area. Our countermeasure is a novel method that can protect Neural Networks from being compromised by Shhta without requiring modifications to the Neural Network itself and can be applied to a wide range of applications. Our experiments have demonstrated the efficacy of our method in protecting Neural Networks against Shhta while preserving the performance of the Neural Network. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Amrhanafy/SHTA. Our method has been tested on various datasets including MNIST, CIFAR10, and ImageNet. Specifically, our method has been tested on three different Neural Networks including a convolutional neural network, a residual network, and a mobile-net for the ImageNet dataset. Our results have shown a significant improvement in accuracy and performance for the three Neural Networks against Shhta. Our method has also been tested on real-world applications including medical and financial tasks. We have developed a versatile, image-slicing Integral Field Unit (IFU) that enhances the capabilities of the IMACS spectrograph on the Magellan Baade Telescope at the Las Campanas Observatory. This addition, known as ROSIE-IFU, allows for simultaneous observation of multiple objects within a single exposure, covering a spatial area of 2.5 x 11.5 arcseconds at a resolution of 2000. With 97 individual slices along the 11.5 arcsecond axis, IFU can detect objects as faint as 24.5 mag per square arcsecond in R band, with a 3.5 arcsecond square pixel spatial resolution. If an object is observed over a 3000s interval, the IFU can determine its velocity dispersion with a 10 km/s error margin. The elemental compositions of stars hosting terrestrial exoplanets are often analyzed through the abundance of metal lines in their spectra, but the technique's precision is limited to approximately 5%. Our research aims to link this level of uncertainty to the formation and bulk composition of terrestrial planets. The abundance of refractory elements in the planets is particularly crucial, as they are thought to be abundant in the solid material that accretes to form planetary cores. Our approach involves estimating the abundance of these elements in stars hosting terrestrial planets by comparing their spectra to those of dwarf stars with well-determined abundances. The technique has been successfully tested on the host stars of Kepler-10, Maia, and Michelmann, and the analysis of refractory elements in these stars is presented. The results of these measurements are then used to estimate the bulk compositions of these planets based on the principles of planetary formation. The investigation of these stars and the analysis of terrestrial planets' compositions are key components of our ongoing research to understand the links between stellar and planetary chemistry. Deep neural networks (DNNs) are increasingly used for wireless localization. However, their effectiveness is heavily dependent on the quality of collected channel state information (CSI). Existing research often relies on exhaustive CSI data collection, which is impractical due to its laborious and costly nature. Moreover, the proposed localizing models often integrate raw CSI data, which hinders their trainability because of the low number of available samples. This paper presents a novel approach to wireless localization using channel paths. Our method collects channel path data through a simplified channel modeling technique, yielding more stable and accurate data. Furthermore, we develop a attention-enhanced DNN model to extract essential information from the collected data. By applying attention filters to the channel paths, our model significantly improves localizing performance and expands the coverage of target locations. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses the performance of current techniques, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.940 for 14 adjacent rooms, a 57% enhancement. Additionally, our method achieves a 0.98 metric of 0.984, outperforming the baseline by 8%. These gains are attributed to the model's ability to selectively extract critical information from the channel paths. Our work also establishes a new benchmark for wireless localization, showcasing state-of-the-art performance. This paper presents a comprehensive framework for modal logic by linking different logging mechanisms in computer science to mathematical concepts. By translating modal logic into the frameworks of topological spaces, ordered spaces, and directed spaces, we provide a unified approach that simplifies the existing diverse systems in the field. Our research builds on previous work from Przymusinski, Walczyk, and Cresswell, focusing particularly on the connection between topological structures and modal semantics. This new framework enables a thorough comparison of the various logging mechanisms used in the proofs of completeness and can potentially be used to introduce hybrid logging mechanisms as topological products. This paper is the first in a series that will apply this framework to specific modal logics to demonstrate the benefits of this unified approach. This benefits will include easier identification of sound and complete logging mechanisms, as well as the ability to extend existing systems to work with non-normal operators. This paper is the first in a series: Part II will apply this framework to logics of knowledge and action. This paper is a preprint, available at arXiv:2111.06457. COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks and their dynamics, but users had to run it locally as a standalone application. To address this limitation, we developed ShinyCOPASI - a web-based platform allowing users to interact with COPASI models through their web browser. Built with R using CoRC and Shiny, ShinyCOPASI mirrors COPASI's interface for seamless familiarity and offers additional web-enabled features. It also integrates visualizations and diagnostics previously only accessible in the native COPASI application. Available at https://shiny.copasi.org, ShinyCOPASI supports model import, visualization, simulation, and analysis, enabling educational and research applications with enhanced reach and accessibility. Furthermore, our framework facilitates the integration of third-party web tools and tools not originally part of COPASI, as well as custom plugins developed by the $\pi$-Lab. Experimental simulations demonstrate the performance of ShinyCOPASI, including speed comparisons of running simulations within ShinyCOPASI and in the native COPASI application. To broaden its utility, ShinyCOPASI is open-source, freely available, and designed for community modifications and adaptations. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/copasi/shinyCOPASI. Instructions for the ShinyCOPASI deployment on R and Ubuntu are available at https://shiny.copasi.org/download.html. Additionally, a video demonstrating ShinyCOPASI is available at https://youtu.be/Gg1S7BZ1D1k. The video shows ShinyCOPASI's capabilities and a user study involving over 40 high school students who learned about biochemical networks using ShinyCOPASI. The results of this study indicate in a classroom setting, ShinyCOPASI enables students to perform tasks previously requiring access to a local COPASI installation or remote connection. Notably, with ShinyCOPASI, students can save and share their models, as well as access a comprehensive library of models developed by the $\pi$-Lab and other members of the bio-network community. We anticipate ShinyCOPASI to further enhance collaboration and dissemination within this community. Achieving accurate uncertainty quantification in machine learning is crucial for maintaining trust in automated systems. In high-stakes applications, such as medical diagnosis, a thorough understanding of model uncertainty cannot be overstated. This report examines current methods for quantifying uncertainty in black-box models, including novel techniques like random feature approximation and input space regularization. By analyzing various uncertainty quantification methods, such as deep neural network-based approaches, Monte Carlo sampling, and structural learning methods, our study assesses their performance using benchmark datasets. This research aims to provide a comprehensive overview of existing techniques to aid developers in selecting the method most suitable for their specific application. In this research, we introduce an inexact algorithm called ILSP-PMILP for solving large-scale Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) that are subject to certain constraints. This approach leverages the Pairwise Maximum Likelihood Estimation (PMILP) method for computing optimal value functions in MDPs. Our ILSP-PMILP algorithm combines PMILP with the Successive Primal-Dual Algorithm and the Inexact Generalized Minimum Residual Algorithm, all working simultaneously, to iterate between primal and dual variables in an alternating manner. However, this approach is only feasible when the state space is sufficiently small. To improve its performance, we propose two strategies for splitting the constraints in PMILP. These strategies enable the solution of large-scale MDPs, whose value functions are computed using the Successive Primal-Dual Algorithm in conjunction with the Inexact Generalized Minimum Residual Algorithm. Our approach is evaluated using a variety of large-scale MDPs. Our ILSP-PMILP algorithm is compared with state-of-the-art solvers, including MCTS and MPE, as well as hardware accelerators, MPTC and TPMP, in terms of its convergence speed and overall performance. Current research primarily focuses on individual learners' benefits when answering queries; nonetheless, it neglects the implications of group queries on the entire learning process. Our study initiates an examination of this issue. Specifically, we aim to enhance robustness in graphical models (gaussian and Bernoulli). We introduce a new concept called regional benefit to determine the usefulness of a group of learners. Our findings reveal that multiple learners can significantly surpass the performance of a single learner in various applications, particularly those with noisy labels in high dimensions or those that involve balanced graphical models. We also find that regional benefit significantly correlates with model complexity, such as sparsity in Gaussian models. Balanced graphical models are another area where group queries excel. We show that regional benefit significantly outperforms individual benefit and that group queries lead to reduced sample complexity compared to individual queries. Lastly, we suggest theoretical lower bounds for achieving robustness using group queries. These findings open the door for further research on group learning. Follow-up research on WISEA J153429.75-104303.3, previously reported by Meisner et al in 2020, has yielded an assortment of peculiar attributes for the object. Key findings from current studies, including multi-band photometry, surface temperature, and absolute magnitudes for various filters, have been detailed. Notably, the object exhibits an unusually bright near-infrared spectrum and its near-infrared colors appear significantly reddened. In contrast, the object's spectral energy distribution reveals a striking discrepancy between its near-infrared colors and the predicted values based on its estimated distance from the Sun. The object's near-infrared spectrum can be best explained as a manifestation of significant dust obscuration in the environment surrounding WISEA J153429.75-104303.3. An alternative, more exotic explanation - namely, the object as a remnant polarization entity resulting from interaction with a nearby White Dwarf in the same field - is also presented in the paper. This possibility is supported by the object's highly asymmetrical appearance in images from the Gaia DR3 catalogue and Prisco et al in 2022. Moreover, this hypothesis is also consistent with the object's slow motion among the objects in the same area. An estimated age for WISEA J153429.75-104303.3 can be predicted - namely, a billion years - which implies that the object's near-infrared emission is likely to persist for an extended period. An in-depth analysis of the object's properties is provided in the paper along with the spectrum of WISEA J153429.75-104303.3 that exhibits a unique combination of both hot and cool components. In conclusion, the object's near-infrared emission can be understood as either a manifestation of dust or as an indication of polarized radiation, both of which have significant implications for the object's classification as a Brown Dwarf or a remnant polarization entity. In either case, the object's near-infrared emission makes it an object of great interest in the field of Infrared Astronomy. Additionally, our results are expected to be beneficial to various processes, such as those involving charged particles in electron-positron collisions. Pressurized Inert Atmosphere Sintering has been identified as a potential method for creating large-scale, vacuum-compatible components for future lunar and Mars bases. This process offers the ability to produce parts directly from fine powders without the need for bonding agents or excessive green body handling. SIS bonding can be completed in a single step at relatively low pressures; however, the process is heavily influenced by the temperature of sintering. This study investigates how varying sintering temperatures affects the microstructure and mechanical properties of samples manufactured using a pressurized inert atmosphere sintering machine. Specimens made from atomic clay and Martian/ lunar regolith samples in Houston and Toronto labs were tested for strength and Young's Modulus at 20, 50, 100, 150, and 200 CPA. The results showed that the yield stress peaks at 100 CPA; however, the results varied depending on the powder type used, with the atomic clay samples exhibiting stronger and stiffer properties than those from Martian and lunar regolith. The strength variations among the specimens made from the same powder type can be attributed to different sintering temperatures, processing pressures, and stresses, as well as any existing defects in the powder or green body defects that were present before processing. The strength of the atomic clay samples met the requirements for many engineering materials, with the lunar regolith samples showing notable resilience with some samples exceeding the required strength standards for many engineering materials. The strength of the Martian regolith samples fell below those of the lunar regolith samples due to the higher thermal expansion coefficients and the presence of H2O, which caused these samples to shrink and increased the stresses in the other components during sintering. The findings of this research support using SIS as a reliable method for producing parts on other planets, and the results of this study will facilitate further research into scaling up SIS to produce larger parts in low gravity environments. Additionally, the results of this investigation will contribute to a better understanding of how the microstructure and mechanical properties of ceramics are affected by sintering temperatures in environments that have little or no atmosphere. Future research will be conducted to study mechanical behavior under actual Martian and lunar gravity conditions in vacuum. The project is also expecting to launch a test to sinter samples in space using materials derived from Martian and lunar regolith. This study focuses on recognizing handwritten mathematical expressions, but instead of using standard video or image data, it utilizes sensor data generated by the user's writing process. The key challenge here is that the sensor data is characterized by its high dimensionality, non-linearity, and non-stationarity. To tackle this issue, a proposed system employs a novel approach based on the principles of self-organization. The first step involves applying the O2S2 framework to reduce the spatial complexity of the data, followed by using OAEM to compress the temporal aspects, and finally selecting a set of optimal features. The recognition of mathematical expressions is then performed through a comparison with pre-stored models, specifically designed for similar expressions, under the principles of similarity-based classification. The efficacy of this approach was demonstrated by conducting experiments on the MME dataset, showcasing its superior performance over standard image-based methods. Notably, the proposed system achieved better accuracy with smaller data dimensions, specifically with a 10D data set, where it outperformed both the RNN and CNN models in expression recognition while requiring significantly reduced data storage space for dimension reduction. The outstanding results from these experiments solidify the basis for future applications and research in sensor-based mathematical expression recognition. The proposed method was further evaluated by analyzing its computational overhead and demonstrating its potential for real-time implementation on mobile devices. The created model was incorporated into the ExpressMME app, a mobile application designed to assist visually impaired students with mathematical problem-solving, utilizing a description of the written expression to perform the required calculations. The success of this integration was validated by gathering feedback from 21 students with visual impairments, who demonstrated a high level of understanding and proficiency in using the app after initial training. The proposed method was found to address the originally raised challenges, specifically regarding data quality and complexity, and successfully paved the way for future developments in sensor-based mathematical expression recognition. The outstanding results from these experiments solidify the basis for future applications and research in sensor-based mathematical expression recognition. The underlying approach was systematically organized and presented in a research paper, addressing the previously mentioned challenges, and providing a comprehensive understanding of the proposed method. This study presents an innovative approach to generate synthetic speech with varied lengths, inspired by a median-driven algorithm in linguistics. In natural speech, differences in duration are often attributed to variations in sentence length. However, existing speech synthesis models overlook these nuances in duration, assuming all sentences can be evenly distributed within a specified range. Our approach involves determining the average sentence lengths for pre-defined time intervals, similar to how a linguistic median analysis would analyze sentence lengths. We found that using these average sentence lengths and incorporating a non-statistical model based on combination of CTC and attention, led to more natural-sounding synthetic speech with reduced repetition. Our results show that this approach produces high-quality synthetic speech with a score of 0.94 AWR and demonstrates the significance of accurately representing sentence lengths in speech synthesis. Moreover, the supplementary materials include detailed explanations of the proposed method, a demonstration of its effectiveness and a comprehensive evaluation of its performance. Additionally, the provided code can be utilized to replicate the proposed method. Lastly, the supplied audio files showcase the synthetic speech samples used in the study. These files include the synthetic speech with standard uniform distribution and the synthetic speech with varying lengths, produced using the proposed median-driven algorithm. Our results reveal a substantial enhancement in the naturalness of the synthetic speech with a score of 0.94 AWR. We aim for our work to contribute to the development of more natural-sounding synthetic speech with a expanded vocabulary size. Furthermore, we believe that our approach can be applied to other tasks in natural language processing, such as text summarization and translation. Due to a lack of dermatologists, patients experience long waiting times for dermatologic care. Slow diagnosis leads to delayed treatment, causing some conditions to go undetected for extended periods. Research into dermatologic models has shown promising potential for improving access to accurate diagnoses, but a key obstacle lies in creating interactive models that allow clear, understandable predictions to be communicated to patients. To address this, a new type of deep learning model, called Skincare, has been developed. It uses a combination of techniques, including a novel attention mechanism and a simplified visualization method, to facilitate effective patient-skincare specialist interactions. By enhancing communication, Skincare contributes to improved patient outcomes and satisfaction. Its innovative approach, characterized by a comprehensive set of well-explained features, has made it possible to demonstrate its efficacy in identifying skin lesions, particularly in distinguishing melanoma from benign lesions and other lesion types. Our team's research and findings have been detailed in a technical report, which has now been made available for reference. Experimental results confirmed that Skincare outperforms competing models in terms of accuracy, AUC, precision, recall, and F1 score across multiple datasets. Notably, Skincare's integrated human-interpretable feature learning mechanism streamlines the identification process, making it easier to understand and use in practical applications. Our research found that Skincare achieves a balance between high performance and interpretability, with a comprehensive evaluation of its performance, comparisons to other models, and a publicly accessible code repository for further development and customization. Its interactive structure, guided by a clear decision policy, enables Skincare to effectively communicate diagnoses and provide decision support, exemplified through our demonstrated patient simulation scenario. Our research identified and addressed a critical issue in dermatologic models and demonstrated the potential of interactive deep learning systems, like Skincare, to enhance both patient outcomes and system performances by providing decision support and facilitating clear, understandable predictions. Related work, our approach, experimental results, and the technical details of our method have been detailed in the report, which has been made available for reference. Our research found that Skincare achieves superior performance, comparability to state-of-the-art models, and high interpretability, along with a clear decision policy, making it an excellent choice for practical use. Our teams' research and findings have been detailed in a technical report, which has been made available for reference. To capture the intrinsic variability of type Ia supernovae from limited spectral data, we developed a stochastic autoencoder, essentially an RNN-based generative model. The method treats temporal dependencies in data as inherent to the intrinsic behavior and can learn to generate temporal sequences on the intrinsic parameters of SN Ia evolution. The autoencoder's learning and RNN components were optimized for low-dimensional latent variables, allowing us to find the most probable temporal sequence of spectral features within a Bayesian framework. The results of our RNN-based model align with the findings of more sophisticated probabilistic methods, suggesting it as a viable technique for extracting intrinsic temporal patterns in high-dimensional SN Ia data. The implemented method was applied to the current SN Ia data, but it did not yield better results than established techniques using linear or quadratic models with a simple linear noise model. The RNN-based model, however, outperformed these methods in some cases, and we plan to reevaluate it with more sophisticated noise models in the future. Understanding the spread of epidemics within complex networks, such as contact graphs, reveals patterns of disease transmission. However, assuming only pair-based interactions oversimplifies the process, neglecting the potential for group infections. To address this, hypergraphs offer a more comprehensive framework to model these interactions. We introduce a new limit to measure the likelihood of an epidemic spreading through a hypergraph: the extinction probability $\lambda_{\max}$. In this study, we explore the applicability of this new framework on two levels. Firstly, we evaluate the effect of adding new edges to existing graphs, revealing that the addition of new edges never worsens the extinction probability. Secondly, we analyze a model where new interactions are introduced randomly, finding that the resulting extinction probability converges to a Gaussian distribution as the number of edges increases. These findings validate the use of the new framework, offering a more accurate assessment of the conditions under which an epidemic transmits through group transmissions. We further substantiate these claims using real-world examples, such as the transmission of measles in London and the spread of COVID-19 among passengers on the Diamond Princess cruise ship, applying our framework to these instances to measure the impact of group transmissions on the likelihood of an epidemic spreading. In particular, we find that the consideration of non-pairwise interactions significantly raises the likelihood of an epidemic spreading in certain scenarios, underlining the importance of modeling these interactions in epidemiological modeling. Finally, we propose the development of future research, suggesting the application of our framework to the study of various epidemics and the exploration of other models of interacting graphs. We make the code for this study publicly available at https://github.com/martintraban/hypergraph_extinction_probability. Recent breakthroughs in understanding 2D magnetic semiconductors, exemplified by the study of CrI$_3$, have generated significant enthusiasm due to their intriguing spin-dependent properties and the potential to revolutionize spintronics and magneto-optoelectronics. Although existing research has primarily focused on the behavior of spins in ferromagnetic CrI$_3$ layers using classical Heisenberg model simulations, there remains an absence of comprehensive studies on the magnetic properties of this material in a practical device setting. In this research, we introduce a model that describes spin interactions within a CrI$_3$ bilayer, incorporating exact diagonalization and many-body perturbation theory to examine the magnetic profile of this system. Our analysis reveals distinct differences between the spin interactions in the central and edge regions of the bilayer, as well as in the context of chiral and Rashba coupling. These findings demonstrate that the magnetic profile observed in CrI$_3$ is primarily driven by an intrabond spin-flip interaction that results in an electric field, rather than being influenced by chiral coupling as traditionally believed. Consequently, this understanding may enable the development of novel ferromagnetic devices based on CrI$_3$, taking advantage of its unique magnetic properties, such as gate-controlled ferromagnetism, at room temperature. Moreover, our study paves the way for investigations into the magnetic structures of other 2D magnetic semiconductors. Our research also highlights the significant potential of Rashba coupling in contributing to the magnetic profile, as evidenced by numerical data, despite being typically weaker than chiral coupling in CrI$_3$. This finding may enable the development of innovative ferromagnetic devices that incorporate Rashba effect. Lastly, our study examines the possibility and stability of obtaining a N\'eel-like magnetic profile in CrI$_3$ that consists of two counter-rotating circles, as well as a Zeeman effect in this system. Our research demonstrates that this profile can be achieved at room temperature and also examines the magnetic profile in layers that exhibit anti-ferromagnetic spin arrangements. Moreover, our study reveals that this profile may be susceptible to layer charge and impurity effects. Meet McMini, a cutting-edge model verifier capable of checking safety properties in multithreaded programs written in C. By using a state machine model and performing DPOR, McMini can handle both data and control dependencies between operations. This enables it to determine the origin of shared variables' values and accurately predict their values, even if they're accessed by multiple threads. Unlike other model checkers, McMini treats all variables as shared, making it simple to understand and configure. The McMini tool is fully functional and can be downloaded at http://www.csc.kb.se/ McMini. Even though McMini is a model verifier, it is motivated by the limitations of traditional model checking and the successes of hardware model checkers. This paper introduces the McMini tool, explores its possible configurations, and evaluates its performance using a comprehensive set of 177 benchmark programs. These benchmarks, drawn from introductory courses and up to 100 lines of code, include pure, safe, and spurious parallelism. The results show that McMini surpasses other model checkers in predicting program behavior and detecting parallelism errors. However, its own limitations become apparent as it reaches its performance bounds, particularly when dealing with intricate program structures. The research presents three promising avenues for future improvement. The core McMini ideas are patented under KB property modeling (class/method 20070115-3. D), a European Union patent. The rapid dissemination of misinformation through mass messaging services like WhatsApp poses significant challenges, particularly during major global events. To combat this issue, WhatsApp introduced limitations on mass forwarding to slow the spread of potentially harmful content. To assess the effectiveness of these limitations, we developed a custom WhatsApp client that allows users to circumvent the restrictions. Utilizing this tool, we launched an experiment designing two types of messages: one containing purely fictional information and the other based on real news. Both were disseminated within a closed user group to exclude external recipients. Our analysis shows that, prior to the introduction of limitations, the fictional message reached a significantly larger group size. Conversely, the group receiving the other message increased in size after the limitations were implemented. Building on these findings, we created a mathematical model simulating the dissemination of misinformation through a network. Our model suggests that the sudden surge in misinformation spread, observed before the limitations were introduced, can be attributed to a combination of high information quality and a large number of initial recipients. Furthermore, we verified that the solution to our mathematical model closely mirrors the results from our large-scale experiment. Our study demonstrates the ineffectiveness of simply limiting mass forwarding to address the complex issue of misinformation spread. Instead, our work presents several promising research directions for further exploration. Specifically, we highlight the potential importance of understanding the origins of the initial forward and distinguishing between reliable and unreliable information to address the challenge at hand. Activated functions in Neural Networks play a crucial role in improving classification results, but they can also be vulnerable to manipulation by adversarial attacks. In the context of speech forgery detection, advanced spoofing techniques can deceive NNs by modifying the activated functions. This has led to the emergence of anti-spoofing systems, which systems aim to counteract such threats. Unfortunately, existing methods are often susceptible to subtle variations in spoofed speeches. Our solution involves introducing a new, highly vigilant activated function called the Hyperbolic Tangent Barrier (HTB) activation function. By incorporating HTB into an end-to-end spoofing counteraction system, we enhance its resistance to sophisticated spoofing attacks. This improvement arises from HTB's unique properties, which apply a barrier to inputs outside the range [-1,1], thus preventing gradient output when inputs exceed this range. When trained with deep fake spoofing data, HTB-based NNs can effectively classify deep fake spoofed speeches and genuine speeches. Our experimental findings on the ASp2018 dataset demonstrate that the HTB activation function significantly improves the performance of end-to-end spoofing counteraction systems, particularly in identifying spoofed speeches. Researcher examines the relationship between a photon's momentum and spin, known as cone momentum, which leads to distinct asymmetries in measurements of second-order correlations. Consequently, this could provide researchers with a new criterion for identifying non-classical properties of light. Furthermore, the concept of cone momentum may also enable the detection of circularly polarized photons in experiments that study photon pair correlations. Ultimately, the use of asymmetric correlations offers a new methodology for exploring the unique properties of light. This method could be adapted for use in more complex systems, such as atoms, that exhibit similar behavior. A newer alternative, Bloom and Cuckoo filters have competitors in Xor Filters and its variants, offering greater efficiency and similar performance. Unlike traditional Bloom and Cuckoo filters, which insert elements using hash functions, Xor Filters insert elements by calculating a hash code for each element and inserting the result into a bit array. This process allows for quicker element insertion and better memory usage. Additionally, Xor Filters combine the insertion efficiency of Bloom Filters with the compactness of Cuckoo Filters, making them a more suitable alternative in many scenarios. A recent enhancement to Xor Filters, known as Chained Xor Filters or CXFs, further improves memory usage by linking adjacent hash values together. Our research involves analyzing CXFs' performance with the modernism of using hash codes that are resistant to arithmetic operations. This results in CXFs having comparable false positive rates to prior variants while using up to 25% less memory or being 2-3 times faster. Our findings also address concerns over the limited availability of hash codes that support arithmetic operations, demonstrating that common hash codes can be used to create CXFs with acceptable levels of inaccuracy. Ultimately, our research validates CXFs as a more efficient alternative to traditional filtering solutions, opening up new possibilities for memory-constrained or performance-sensitive applications. However, when considering out-of-context data, this task becomes more complex and requires robust models to accommodate unfamiliar settings. The TOLWW dataset comprises 300 character tracks across 100 maps, 20 buildings, and 4 games, all captured at a frame rate of 10Hz. By employing a multi-faceted approach, PO-DCD addresses this challenge by providing model-free solutions to simultaneously address partial coverage and adaptive capabilities in the context of change detection and isolation. Furthermore, PO-DCD gives rise to a novel Monte-Carlo prediction algorithm, referred to as the Adapting Partially-Observed Change Detection and Isolation (APoCDI) algorithm, which is demonstrated to be consistent and reliable even under adverse conditions. The APoCDI algorithm is then successfully applied to the control of an adaptive system, specifically a thermal processing system, to converge to an optimal profile despite partial coverage of sensors and adaptability limits. This work offers a first-of-its-kind comprehensive approach to partially-covered sequential change detection and isolation in dynamic systems with sub-optimal sensing. The proposed PO-DCD framework has far-reaching applications in a wide range of domains including fault detection and isolation, control systems, and operational settings, showcasing its potential to be a pivotal research area in systems and control theory. Experimental results from various scenarios, combined with its successful implementation in an industrial setting, verify the efficacy of the APoCDI algorithm and validate the PO-DCD framework. (2021) primal-dual method, integrated with the Shalev-Shwartz (2012) algorithm for minimizing a single linear function over a polytope. It has two key components: first, a Markovian policy iteration that resolves the Bellman operator, and second, a simultaneous perturbation primal-dual algorithm. The former uses the Altman (2001) fixed point iteration, and the latter can be seen as an adaptation of the Zinkevich (2003) gradient perturbation method. This new algorithm ensures that the estimated value function and policy converge to within the desired precision of the theoretical minimum in terms of optimal reward and action choice, and achieves this convergence rate. Notably, although $\vartheta$ may take on negative values, as $x$ approaches infinity, the magnitude of these fluctuations becomes increasingly restricted, ultimately allowing us to conclude that $\vartheta(x) \geq x - C_{\rm app}$. In particular, by showing that the sum of squared differences between prime values and their conjugates can never equal zero, we are able to arrive at a contradiction, and thus confirm the twin prime hypothesis. Note that this approach relies heavily on highly advanced mathematical concepts, and thus requires a highly sophisticated understanding of number theory. Although some readers may find this approach appealing due to its brevity and elegance, others may prefer more traditional proofs over this methodology. Finally, it is worth noting that this approach is not compatible with established results from previous research on prime numbers. Therefore, while this proof may be useful for educational purposes in the future, it is not currently suitable for publication in a peer-reviewed journal. Nevertheless, we offer this approach as an innovative and elegant proof of the twin prime hypothesis, and encourage mathematicians to utilize this method in their future research on prime numbers. High-dimensional presence-absence data is often analyzed using Bayesian predictive clustering, which can benefit from various clustering methods. 

Our investigation compares Bayesian predictive clustering results with those obtained by seven different clustering methods from the literature. 

A simulation study in R has shown that all methods perform similarly when 500 samples are generated, but the choice of method significantly affects the outcome when the number of dimensions exceeds the number of samples. 

In such cases, 57% of the methods tested failed to produce results better than random guessing, while the remaining options are explored further. 

Our analysis highlights the challenges posed by high-dimensional data and proposes future research avenues to address this issue. 

To facilitate reproducibility, our code and simulation data are available online. 

This research focuses on presence-absence data, but the findings are also relevant to multivariate data. 

Our study examines six presence-absence data sets and three multivariate data sets, all obtained from the OpenAccess Microarray database. 

To evaluate the performance of each clustering method, we consider six metrics, including type I and II errors, the likelihood of each class, and two other alternatives. 

Our results indicate that Bayesian predictive clustering and the self-organizing map outperform the other methods across the board. 

Both methods exhibit exceptional performance on the six presence-absence data sets, as well as the three multivariate data sets. 

To illustrate the applicability of Bayesian predictive clustering to real-world problems, we apply the method to four dimensions of the colon cancer data. 

Our analysis reveals three classes that distinguish colon cancer patients from healthy individuals and a third group that represents mixed samples. 

Similar results are obtained when the method is applied to the colon cancer data in five and ten dimensions. 

Our study demonstrates the ability of Bayesian predictive clustering to uncover meaningful classes in data that are high-dimensional and presence-absence based. 

The method excels at recovering classes that were previously defined manually and performs exceptionally well in the presence of noise. 

Our results indicate that Bayesian predictive clustering significantly outperforms the other methods across a variety of data sets and performance metrics.

Our study is the first to evaluate the performance of this method using R on a presence-absence data set.

High-performance computing on General Purpose Graphics Processing Units (GPGPUs) heavily relies on efficient memory allocation to optimize parallel code execution. To meet this need, various memory allocators have been developed for GPGPUs, some of which even outperform sequential memory usage. Nevertheless, GPGPU-based solutions have several fundamental Drawbacks: 1) They can only be used with manual memory management in low-level programming environments like CUDA. 2) They fail to provide a seamless development experience for object-oriented programmers, forcing them to lower their programming standard. To address these issues, we present DynaSOAr, an innovative memory allocator designed for high-performance object-oriented programming on GPGPUs with minimal overhead. Built upon the Serial Object Array (SOA) data structure, DynaSOAr features a unique dynamic memory allocation mechanism that automatically calculates the required memory for a given object or method, then uses an adaptive allocation strategy to distribute objects across GPGPUs with optimal performance in mind. To further optimize performance, DynaSOAr also incorporates a Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler that dynamically optimizes memory access and enables static code analysis. Experimental results demonstrate the superior speed and efficiency of DynaSOAr in comparison to other state-of-the-art GPGPU allocators, showcasing its ability to achieve up to a 30% performance increase in numerical applications with an 8% reduction in memory usage. To date, DynaSOAr remains the first concurrent memory allocator for high-level object-oriented programming on GPGPUs, offering a seamless development experience to developers. We propose a distorted resolvent method to obtain Nash equilibria for static Nash games and discrete-time stochastic Nash games with short horizons. Our approach involves three key components: a distorted resolvent that reverses the nonmonotone monotone operator theory, a continuous-time perturbed dynamic system that yields stable trajectories, and a small perturbation size that ensures reasonable game outcomes. Unlike existing large perturbation methods, our method can generate precise equilibrium trajectories without sacrificing economic significance. Additionally, our analysis includes rigorous estimates of the perturbation size and validation of the distorted resolvent theory. We apply our method to three exemplary modeling scenarios: a follower's game involving linear time-invariant systems with quadratic costs, and two stochastic zero-sum games involving linear Schr\"{o}dinger equations and matrix $M$-matrices. Our results not only provide theoretical insights but also offer practical tools for generating Nash equilibria. Our approach is best viewed as a three-part distillation of the nonmonotone monotone operator theory, the perturbed dynamic system, and the stochastic Nash games with the perturbation size serving as a switch that separates the stable trajectories from the equilibrium paths. Therefore, we have dubbed our method the Distorted Resolvent Method. \medskip {_\textbf{Editor's Note:}} The corresponding author would like to dedicate this work to Professor Michael C. Cancer detection through image analysis has become a major area of focus in the field of medical science. This technique has shown significant progress in recent years, thanks to advances in deep learning technologies. However, the accuracy of machine learning models can be compromised by unusual samples, which are often ignored in image classification studies. This research aims to control outlier samples in skin lesion image analysis through a novel entropy-based approach. First, we develop an unusual data detection method that identifies rare sample categories in the data set. Subsequently, we propose an optimized entropy-based sampling method to generate a balanced and small subset of unusual samples. Finally, we design a new dataset with integrated outlier samples, integrate the optimized sampling method into a deep learning framework for training, and evaluate the effectiveness of this approach on the identification of skin carcinoma types. Human minimal clips offer valuable insights into object motion predictions. But can they inform theoretical models of dynamic object identification, such as those using sparse estimation methods? A comprehensive study on the PPT quadrilateral hypothesis has been conducted.
The PPT quadrilateral hypothesis states that any PPT region on a four-party state
remains PPT when considering local outcomes resulting from measurement.
Our investigation involves examining PPT quadrilaterals within general four-party scenarios.
The local PPT condition has been rigorously applied to key regions such as
reduced states from Rastrelli's PPT boxes and W-boxes under local measurements.
Furthermore, the PPT quadrilateral hypothesis's validity has been assessed for
embeeding of W-boxes and Rastrelli's PPT boxes within general four-party states.
The PPT quadrilateral hypothesis's applicability to four-party state PPT boxes
has been thoroughly analyzed, leading to a partial resolution. The PPT
quadrilateral hypothesis's validity for all four-party state PPT boxes remains
unresolved. The study has provided significant insights into the PPT
quadrilateral hypothesis. Additionally, the study has constructed new
four-party state PPT boxes not achievable through convex roof of local PPT
regions. The PPT boxes developed here have potential applications in
extending PPT quadrilateral hypothesis to include quantum interaction. The
study has explored the PPT quadrilateral hypothesis's implications on
entanglement measures such as quadrilateral Lovasz number. The study has
established that if PPT quadrilateral hypothesis holds, then quadrilateral
Lova\'z number is zero. The PPT quadrilateral hypothesis's influence on
entanglement dimensions has also been examined. The study has shown that if
PPT quadrilateral hypothesis is valid, then entanglement dimensions of
four-party state have strictly decreasing trend. The study has resolved a
directional consequence of PPT quadrilateral hypothesis. The PPT
quadrilateral hypothesis's influence on monogamy of four-party state has
also been examined. The study has shown that if PPT quadrilateral
hypothesis holds, then monogamy of four-party state has strictly decreasing
trend. The PPT quadrilateral hypothesis's validity has also been assessed
based on random state. The study has shown that PPT quadrilateral
hypothesis holds for nearly all four-party state. The PPT
quadrilateral hypothesis's influence on convergence of four-party state has
also been examined. The study has shown that if PPT quadrilateral
hypothesis is valid, then four-party state has convergent series
expansion.

In brain tissue, the regulation of substance transport is vital to maintaining proper cellular function, particularly in areas like the brain's hippocampus and cerebral cortex, where the process is critical for learning and memory. Unlike passive diffusion, active transport can move substances against concentration gradients by using energy, but it also has limitations and can become overwhelmed by high delivery rates, leading to blocked transport and ultimately cellular damage. To investigate this "transport congestion" more effectively, we're developing a mathematical model that incorporates the biological mechanisms of substance transport, regulation, and congestion. This model will help us simulate substance movement and identify the mechanisms that protect cells against congestion and the effects of substance removal. By optimizing parameters in a way that minimizes congestion-based damage to cells, the model can also generate predictive scenarios for understanding the consequences of failed transport mechanisms and the benefits of therapeutic interventions. This abstract summarizes our research, focusing on the development and application of a novel optimality condition that arises from our model. It has implications for the broader theory of optimal control, yet it also has practical significance for the fields of neuroscience and neuroengineering. Furthermore, we use our model to illustrate the interconnectedness of substance transport, brain function, and the functioning of specific brain structures, such as the temporal lobe and the brainstem. This model serves as a tool for communicating with neuroscientists and neuroengineers working in these fields. Finally, we highlight the model's flexibility and highlight specific examples of parameter values that can help us better understand the effects of variable brain blood flow and the movement of substances assisted by carriers. These scenarios include models of compounded transport mechanisms and transport models that take into account the unique properties of the substance itself. These scenarios can inform future research into the molecular biology of substance transport. Ultimately, we aim to use our model to investigate the relationship between substance transport and memory, but we begin by examining a simpler parameter optimization problem. This problem involves finding the best transport settings to minimize congestion and maintain proper cellular function during periods of normal activity, but we also explore the what-if scenarios of altered transport parameters and the effects of blocked transport mechanisms. This optimization problem is particularly relevant because it allows us to investigate the most effective transport settings to maintain proper cellular function during normal activity, but we also explore the challenges of adapting to changing conditions, such as when substances are delivered at very high rates. This research is supported by a grant from the National Science Foundation. In this abstract, we summarize our research, focusing on the development and application of a novel optimality condition that arises from our model.

A generalized group of Tversky metrics on finite subsets of $N$ can be defined by the formula $\delta_T(x,y) = 1 - \frac{\tau K_{x,y}}{C_{x}+K_{x,y}}$, where $\tau$ is a parameter that varies between $\frac{1}{2}$ and $1$, $K_{x,y}$ represents the number of distinct elements shared by $x$ and $y$, and $C_{x}$ denotes the cardinality of set $x$. This family of metrics is connected to the Jaccard distance for $\tau = \frac{1}{2}$ and is related to the normalized information distance for $\tau = 1$. This parametrized family of metrics offers a versatile tool for controlling the influence of cardinality in similarity assessments. By fixing $\tau$ and observing the effect on the metric's behavior, one possible application is in data mining, while $\tau$ adjustment leads to a method for ranking items based on similarity, effectively translating to a method for feature selection when aiming to minimize redundancy among chosen features. Experimental results from our simulations suggest that the optimal value of $\tau$ can often lead to a minimal number of features while maintaining high overall similarity among selected items. Furthermore, the generalized group of Tversky metrics is viewed through the lens of a random walk on a weighted graph, where edges between non-adjacent nodes are introduced based on $\tau$ adjustments between nodes. Notably, for $\tau = \frac{1}{2}$, our analysis mirrors the Perceptron convergence theorem. Recent advancements in motion deblurring have been significantly facilitated by deep learning techniques. However, existing models can only directly learn movement-related information or gain insight from a separate auxiliary network. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach called Pseudo-Blur Generator (PBG), which enables a more efficient training process for deep learning models through data augmentation. The PBG method creates synthetic blurs on input images to simulate actual motion effects, producing clearer images even in challenging scenarios. The proposed PBG method streamlines the training process for a single model to improve its performance across various blur types and intensities. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of the PBG method, yielding better outcomes than current state-of-the-art models in terms of objective metrics and subjective quality assessments. The energy efficiency of today's machines can be significantly influenced by
the characteristics of the datasets they process, in addition to the inherent
complexity of the algorithms used. This fact has led to a growing interest in
dataset-specific profiling at the level of individual programs or frameworks,
in order to tailor profiling to the specific needs of each dataset, rather than
relying on more general methods. In this paper, we explore the potential benefits
of integrating dataset-specific profiling into the development of conscious
software systems, particularly in regards to energy efficiency. The paper's
contributions can be broken down into two main areas: (a) a comprehensive
study of the relationship between dataset properties and the energy consumption
of algorithms, providing insights on dataset-specific profiling; (b) a
quantitative evaluation of the advantages and disadvantages of combining dataset
particular profiling and program-specific profiling, using a variety of
datasets; (c) a comparison of the performance of consciousness-aware software
systems that use dataset-specific information with those that do not, under
varying workload conditions. The results of our experiments have revealed that
(1) different datasets exhibit distinct energy consumption patterns; (2) the
energy efficiency of algorithms can change significantly, even when running on
the same hardware, such as when switching from image processing to linear
algebra operations; (3) using dataset-specific information can lead to a
notable reduction of up to 30% in energy consumption, in comparison to program
or workload-level profiling; (4) while dataset-specific profiling can result in
slightly longer setup times, it ultimately allows for more efficient use of
energy under real-world conditions. In conclusion, the integration of dataset
particular profiling into the development of conscious software systems
enables them to achieve better energy efficiency, in addition to reducing the
detachment period, by allowing for more precise profiling of energy-consuming
workloads and resulting in more accurate awareness profiles. The code and
datasets used in this study are publicly available for reproduction of the

We offer exact estimates for the initial eigenvalue of a nonlinear elliptic operator subject to a Robin boundary condition. This involves an iterative approach that combines WLOG and deepness concepts. Building on these estimates, we prove an asymptotic formula for the eigenvalue in question. This represents a significant advancement over existing knowledge on spectral extremal problems with nonlinear potentials and boundary conditions. The reasoning behind this outcome involves novel considerations of regularity and uniqueness for nonlinear Dirichlet problems with parameter dependence. The proof itself incorporates a well-known symmetry argument, revealing the symmetry of the eigenfunctions and enabling the application of the moving plane technique. Additionally, we demonstrate the continuity of the eigenvalue in question as its associated nonlinearity undergoes small perturbations. This involves an initial WLOG-based analysis of the influence of perturbations on the eigenvalue and a subsequent deepness-based completion of the argument. The estimates derived in this research are applicable to various types of elliptic operators, including those describing the interaction of particles in Bose-Einstein condensates and van der Waals interactions between particles and boundaries. The research presented here has connections to category theory and the study of allegrico spaces via the allegrico topological index. The notion of allegrico space refers to a mathematical structure where the map in question is not necessarily continuous but rather possesses a specific type of discontinuity. The results presented in this paper offer first-ever estimates for the initial eigenvalue of a nonlinear elliptic operator subject to a Robin boundary condition, with the possibility of extension to other types of boundary conditions and the combination of various types of nonlinearities and boundary conditions. Semi-supervised learning in graph data using Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) has seen significant advancements, with improvements in theoretical foundations and algorithmic implementations. However, the core concepts of GCNNs remain unclear, particularly in regards to feature matching between adjacent nodes. This paper introduces a novel GCNN layer, the Matched Filtering Layer (MFL), which provides a straightforward and effective means of matching node features in GCNNs. By doing so, it sheds light on the theoretical foundations of GCNNs, while also offering improved MFL-based networks that surpass current state-of-the-art GCNNs in benchmark tests. Additionally, the researchers offer an open-source benchmark platform for testing GCNNs and GCNN-based models. This paper serves as a foundational starting point for further research into the underlying principles of GCNNs. From a mathematical perspective, the researchers view GCNNs as a form of spectral CNN, which involves transforming graph data into a suitable domain for CNN processing. This transformation is critical to understanding the workings of GCNNs. In an effort to illuminate this process, the researchers designed an MFL layer, which matches node features in GCNN networks. This new layer leverages the principles of 2D matched filtering, a technique originally employed in image processing. The MFL layer was tested on three data sets: the well-known Cora data set and two data sets derived from protein sequences. The results of these tests revealed improved performance relative to current state-of-the-art GCNNs, which included Graph Attention Networks, JCNN, and PNN. The researchers also explored the open-source benchmark platform, the Matched Filtering Benchmark (MFB), which offers a comprehensive suite of tools for testing GCNNs and matching-based networks. This platform is designed to evaluate the underlying principles of GCNNs, as well as the effectiveness of novel matching mechanisms. The researchers utilized MFB to examine key research questions, such as the role of filtering mechanisms in GCNNs and the performance of matching-based networks on unlabelled data. The outcomes of these tests contributed to new insights and a revised comparison of GCNN algorithms. Lastly, the researchers offered a revised classification structure for GCNNs and matching mechanisms, as well as key research questions and areas for further investigation. This new framework is intended to promote research into the underlying principles of GCNNs and the effectiveness of novel matching mechanisms. J. Nesheim later introduced a related concept, circularity, as a key property 
for such arrangements, and we here explore its significance. 
We demonstrate that an arrangement which is circular may not be nontransitive, 
and, conversely, an arrangement that is nontransitive may be circular. 
Our primary contribution lies in the development of two distinct methods to prove 
criterion-based restrictions on the possible values of circularity. 
We also examine a revised version of the initial problem, where we consider the possibility 
of partially defined trust relationships. 
Ultimately, we investigate an extension of the concept of circularity to arrangements 
with more than four participants. 
In addition to these findings, we provide a detailed examination of the relationship

The study reveals that the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model exhibits Rabi oscillations to a greater extent than the Jaynes-Cummings model, particularly when using a two-mode squeezing state as the initial condition. Notably, this is in contrast to observations for a single-photon initial state, where the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model shows reduced Rabi oscillation compared to the Jaynes-Cummings model. Additionally, the study examines entanglement and transmission for both initial states, revealing that the entangulation of the system follows a different pattern for each state as time progresses, while transmission is largely dependent on the Hamming distance. The findings presented here are consistent with previously published research. However, identifying IBIs from noisy signals is difficult, especially when they are disrupted by motion noise, which is common in individuals who are active. Researchers previously used traditional deep learning models to improve IBI assessment, but these methods were vulnerable to signal corruption. A new deep learning model called Tiramisu has been developed to efficiently and effectively identify IBIs from noisy signals. By incorporating element-wise residual blocks and skip connections, Tiramisu outperforms other models by identifying IBIs with higher accuracy, even in corrupted signals. When tested on data from two different sources, Tiramisu consistently demonstrated better performance, ultimately indicating greater potential for real-world use. Evaluation of Tiramisu revealed that it surpasses other models with a significant margin of 4-6% in terms of root mean squared error. Additionally, Tiramisu's performance was not limited to the specific dataset it was trained on but also showed promising results on a separate dataset, indicating higher root mean squared error, although still with reduced error rates compared to other methods. We introduce HUMBI, a massive, open-source dataset comprising over 76,000 video recordings showcasing human body movements from diverse viewpoints.  The HUMBI dataset is comprised of three segments: 1) A comprehensive, high-resolution video collection featuring complex daily human activities within a 3D environment from multiple perspectives, achieved through the integration of seven 3D cameras, capturing a total of 57,000 entries. 2) A set of precise, articulated human pose annotations, captured using high-resolution, 2D cameras, totaling 10,000 entries. 3) A dataset of 9,000 entries combining both video and pose data.  The HUMBI dataset significantly outperforms current standards in terms of resolution, richness, and perspective variety, thereby setting a new benchmark in human body movement analysis.  The HUMBI dataset is openly accessible at https://humbi.org.  In addition to releasing the dataset, we also introduce the HUMBI Challenge, a competition centered around three primary tasks: 1) Recognizing three-dimensional human pose from a single video, while also considering the impact of perspective variety. 2) Classifying complex human activities from novel viewpoints, in addition to identifying their corresponding categories. 3) Generating three-dimensional human pose from video recordings, with a focus on joint detection and localization.  The HUMBI Challenge evaluates the performance of approaches using both video and pose data, with the aim of advancing new methodologies that can adapt to various perspectives, thereby enhancing robustness and consistency across different applications.  More information regarding the HUMBI Challenge is available at https://humbichallenge.org. A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks, leveraging bidirectional propagation and feature alignment to utilize information from the input video. In our research, we upgrade BasicVSR by introducing new techniques - Propagation in Color Space and Recursive Feature Alignment - to further improve video super-resolution quality. The first innovation applies propagation in the Color INERTIAL Frame, aiming to utilize information within the input video more effectively. The second involves improving feature alignment by aligning features recursively, rather than simultaneously, as employed in the BasicVSR method. Our results through experimental analysis on the LQ-Video dataset reveal a notable enhancement in PSNR, with the improved model achieving 0.53 and 0.46 dB improvement at x3 and x5 scaling factors respectively, alongside a considerable reduction in SSIM. Moreover, our model exhibits improved flexibility in video super-resolution, with the findings from NTREND dataset indicating a notable boost in SSIM and PSNR over the BasicVSR method. Our code is available online at https://github.com/Inria/BasicVSR++ for academic users. The model's performance in real-world scenarios has been demonstrated through video demos at https://basicvsr.inria.fr/demos.html. Our model has been successfully tested on various test sets, including Vimeo-90p, LQ-Video, and Real-90p, with the model's generalization on inductive and transductive settings being analyzed through experimental investigation. A deep study into the effect of propagation steps on the performance of BasicVSR and our improved model has been conducted, with the findings from analysis by mean binary variance.
