In multi-task reinforcement learning, using a shared representation can help learn tasks more efficiently, but it can also cause problems if different tasks interfere with each other. We investigated how this interference affects learning in a model-based multi-task setting, and found that using a single global model to represent tasks as a distribution over possible environments can lead to the outcome where no task can be learned optimally. We then presented several modular approaches to multi-task reinforcement learning that overcome this issue by representing each task in a separate model. These methods demonstrate significant improvements over existing methods on challenging multi-task environments. Furthermore, our methods have the benefit of being more interpretable as they allow for the identification of distinct structures in different tasks. Overall, our results show that using separate models for different tasks can help learn these tasks more effectively and prevent destructive interference. Additionally, our method allows for the discovery of multiple underlying structures in a set of related tasks. A public demonstration of the models' structure is available at https://mirl.github.io/mt-rl. Additionally, the code for replicating the results is available at https://github.com/mirl/modular-mt-rl.

Due to the fundamental trade-off between energy production and entropy generation, the performance of any heat engine is severely limited, regardless of its technology or theoretical framework. In our study, we explore the maximum work output of an ideal four-stroke heat engine with access to heat baths of two different temperatures and extensive control over the cooling and expansion phases. By optimizing the engine's cycle, we identify the most efficient designs that effectively extract work from the system and find that work output is directly proportional to the temperature difference, a finding applicable to engines of any size. Furthermore, our research reveals that achieving maximum efficiency in these systems requires sophisticated yet predictable adjustments in the engine's mechanical and thermal components, characteristics that could facilitate the development of highly efficient thermal machines at the macro and micro scales. Additionally, our study provides a framework for optimizing thermal cycles in systems that interact with multiple heat baths and could be applied to a range of thermal phenomena and biological processes, such as muscle contraction, that have been found to have similar mechanisms and a limited number of controllable components. It is our hope that this research will contribute to the advancement of advanced thermal technologies and help in understanding biophysical processes, such as muscle contraction, at the level of cells and organisms. Finally, we observe that our findings on restricted control are relevant to studies of muscle contraction, where the maximum work output generated by an actin-myosin model that interacts with two heat baths and has a limited number of controllable components is found to be directly proportional to the temperature difference, a relationship that agrees with previously collected experimental data. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity and unbiased audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven approach of WN lead to difficulties in tuning pitch. To overcome this, QPNet leverages prior knowledge by integrating a pitch-sensitive dilated convolution layer into WN. Experimental evaluations of QPNet on Melcepstral features and raw waveforms demonstrate improved low-variance pitch estimations with fewer network parameters, as well as comparable audio quality and unconditional perceptual metrics to state-of-the-art WN models. Additionally, the proposed model exhibits reduced training and sampling complexities. Notably, QPNet achieves the 0.91 MER goal on the VCTK dataset, outperforming base WN with a 0.07 improvement. Related code and pre-trained models are available on GitHub at the link provided. This work is inspired by the 2019 WaveNet challenge and our research follows the established evaluation procedures. Valuable insights and suggestions from the community are appreciated. 

Keywords: Quasi-Periodic WaveNet, WaveNet, raw waveform generation, pitch-controlled, low-variance pitch estimation, network architecture design, training and sampling complexity, evalution metrics and methods, VCTK dataset, Wavenet challenge.

Existing approaches to image tone mapping, a technique to reduce image brightness, are largely limited to their original colors and don't account for changes in lighting. This means they fail to produce natural-looking images when applied to scenes with different lighting configurations. To address this, we've developed a new method for extracting a style from pairs of images, allowing for the creation of universal tone mapping algorithms for both brightening and dimming. This style extraction method, based on the architecture of pre-trained networks, identifies the specific components of the image that are affected by the lighting. By applying it to pairs of forward and reverse tone mapping images, our method captures the inherent patterns of each lighting configuration. This means that when applied to scenes with new lighting configurations, our method produces images with natural-looking colors and a realistic tone. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we've tested it on a range of scene types and compared the results to existing methods, showing that our method produces images with more natural colors and a more realistic tone. Additionally, our method performs better when handling scenes with complex structures and objects. All of our source code and datasets are publicly available, and we've also released the trained models for both forward and reverse tone mapping algorithms. These models can be used for reducing image brightness or changing the image colors to simulate different lighting configurations. To our knowledge, this is the first method that can automatically learn the image styles from pairs of images and the corresponding lighting configurations, and the resulting models have performed better than existing methods in both forward and reverse tone mapping applications. Ultimately, our method has demonstrated that it's possible to design a single tone mapping algorithm that can automatically change image colors to match a wide range of lighting configurations, both natural and artificial. This geometry hypergraph, which incorporates a specific spiral-like structure, showcases a complex distribution of its cliques and highlights the limitations of vertex-stability in guaranteeing a straightforward structure. The atomic mass radius (R$_{\rm AMR}$) and the tensor-averaged mean field (TAMF) radius are two important parameters that help understand nuclear structure. The formation of $^{6}$Li and $^{7}$Li through the $^{6}$Li+$^{51}$V elastic scattering reaction allows researchers to determine the R$_{\rm AMR}$ and TAMF of $^{51}$V, as well as its electronic scattering radius. The experimental data collected by using a dedicated lithium beam facility, known as the lithium beam tandem (LBT), is supported by a finite range residue calculus (FRRRC) method which incorporates the correct behavior of the low-energy Coulomb parameter (y-parameter) for low-energy proton-proton scattering. The yield of the reaction was measured by detecting both lithium and xenon reaction products, allowing researchers to obtain experimental cross-sections. The observed yield can be divided into an angular momentum projected cross-section and a d-state yield, which were determined by analyzing the angular distribution of the lithium reaction products, thereby confirming the existing knowledge on d-state parameters, or by correcting existing d-state parameters based on a novel analysis technique that compares observed and calculated cross-sections using a microscopic framework. Furthermore, the reaction data was used to validate and refine the finite range residue calculus (FRRRC) method for low-energy proton-proton scattering, which was achieved by comparing calculated and experimental cross-sections of the $^{6}$Li+$^{51}$V elastic scattering reaction. Finally, the reaction data was compared with theoretical results from the eFT and TAMF models, which were developed to understand the Li-Be isotopic anomaly, as well as the d-state yields of $^{6,7}$Li. A snake-like robot design, influenced by the Pacific eel, allows it to move effectively on flat surfaces by contracting its body and using its tail to propel itself forward. This unique 'walking' motion, which doesn't require external support, is made possible by stabilizing forces that maintain the robot's center of gravity over its base. By integrating a gimbal in its head, this eel-inspired robot can navigate horizontal surfaces with stability, demonstrating an average speed of 14 cm per second on a rough surface and 24 cm per second on a smooth surface. Additionally, its climbing ability has been optimized by refining the robot's tail and modal transitions, which have led to notable performance enhancements. Evaluations have shown that the optimized robot can maintain a vertical posture, move in both forward and reverse directions, and even climb inclined surfaces with up to 45 degrees of angle with success. Moreover, its climbing speed has been improved to 6.8 cm per second on a rough surface and 9.8 cm per second on a smooth surface. All of these advancements have been thoroughly evaluated on a custom-made eel-inspired robot called 'Ophelia'. Research findings indicate that an eel-inspired robot design is highly suitable for a variety of challenging environments, such as search and rescue operations in uneven terrain and potentially hostile environments like Chernobyl, which could be depicted in a simulated 'Chernobyl Challenge'. This research not only presents an innovative robot design but also a set of complex challenges, with the 'Chernobyl Challenge' being one of the most demanding tasks to date. This paper outlines a groundbreaking method for optimizing wireless communication networks using D2D technology, specifically in scenarios involving video sharing applications. Traditional scheduling approaches used in traditional cellular networks are inadequate for D2D networks due to their focus on cellular coverage, neglecting factors essential to D2D video sharing, such as link duration and video quality. To address this gap, we propose a novel scheduling method which balances video transmission delay against overall network congestion. Our approach involves converting the D2D link establishment process into a machine learning problem, using an advanced deep learning technique to train a model which can quickly predict optimal scheduling options. Our simulation results demonstrate that this method significantly enhances the network's capacity to handle video sharing demands while maintaining low end-to-end delay. Moreover, we show that this model retains its performance even when subjected to channel and interference conditions differing from those experienced during the training phase. To evaluate the efficiency of this approach, we compared its performance to that of more conventional scheduling strategies, revealing that our method yields substantial gains in terms of increased successful transmission rates and improved network utilization. Specifically, our results indicate that this deep learning-based scheduling method achieves a 30.88% to 41.42% boost in network capacity, depending on the specific system configuration. Moreover, we found that this approach leads to a 0.32 to 0.47 times reduction in end-to-end delay, further highlighting the method's effectiveness in D2D video sharing scenarios. To showcase the model's adaptability, we also conducted additional simulations in which the network's channel conditions suddenly changed, prompting the model to adjust its scheduling decisions in real-time in response to this change. Our analysis shows that this deep learning-based method is capable of rapidly adapting to such shifts, maintaining its performance even under these dynamic conditions. To further validate the model's value, we calculated the break-even points for which the model's performance would be deemed satisfactory. Our results indicate that this approach would be considered successful when the network experiences an average congestion level of 0.38 and an average interference level of 1.13. To summarize, we have developed a deep learning-based scheduling method for D2D video sharing networks, specifically designed to optimize D2D link establishment and counteract the network's congestion and interference. A new concept for generating intense, coherent X-rays has been developed using a technique called "multiplexing", which involves stacking many laser modes into a short period of time. The effectiveness of this approach, specifically for a free-electron laser oscillator, has been evaluated and compared with traditional free-electron laser technology. Our research revealed that, at a similar level of technical complexity, multiplexing offers significant enhancements to key performance indicators, resulting in a considerable amplification of laser energy and a notable increase in the coherence of the X-ray beam, leading to a substantial improvement in the overall brightness of the X-ray output. Furthermore, our findings showed that nearly full energy transfer from the oscillator can be achieved, unlike in traditional free-electron laser designs where a substantial amount of energy is lost due to the "micro-bunching" process. An example simulation of the gain mechanism in a 1.5 nm X-ray line demonstrates the feasibility of obtaining one femtosecond, 10 keV X-ray pulses at a rate of 100 kHz from an FEO using a conventional undulator of just 10 meters in length. Our study also identifies specific technical limitations that hinder further improvements in performance, particularly a finite electron bunch length and beam dilution during amplification, which could be addressed by employing a shorter undulator or an electron storage ring. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that, at a similar level of technical complexity, multiplexing offers a substantial improvement in the coherence and brightness of X-ray free-electron laser outputs, making it a crucial concept for the development of next-generation, high-intensity X-ray sources. Additionally, our study shows that, in practice, a major enhancement in the coherence of the X-ray output is within reach in the current, fourth-generation, 3rd harmonic generation X-ray laser facility, and in many cases, a considerable improvement in its brightness can also be achieved. Our findings are expected to be valuable to researchers working on free-electron laser X-ray lasers and other areas of laser-matter interaction and high-intensity radiation source applications. We address this issue using a graph-theoretic approach by considering a special type of network, M-dimensional multidigraph, to analyze how an adversary could derive information from a source output, given a cover set's knowledge. We also explore the problem of determining the least restrictive cover set constraints required to prevent adverse outcomes and find that this can be achieved through the concept of source sigma-schemas. We relate this excess to the spectrum of its Gram matrix and the alpha invariant of its unit circle. We also study how an adversary can extract information from a source output, given a cover set's knowledge, in non-regular languages and identify the entropy limit excess for these languages. Deep learning-based approaches for enhancing low-resolution Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) images performance has a constrained applicability in real-world scenarios due to their need for a large amount of high-resolution SAR images in training, which is often unavailable in practice. Traditional supervised methods can also only provide local improvements. An emerging Supers-resolution technique called Deep Learning-based SAR image enhancement (DL-SARE) attempts to bridge this gap by learning a high-resolution image from low-resolution SAR images, though it still relies on paired LR and HR image pairs for supervision and suffers from degradation in image quality when paired data is not available. Our MrSARP model, which employs a hierarchical generative structure in the form of a Precedent, offers a solution to this problem by generating high-resolution SAR images from LR images in a series of forward passes, resulting in an autoencoder-like effect that also learns a variational autoencoder (VAE). The MrSARP model outperforms current DL-SARE techniques by achieving better super-resolution performance and preserving more inherent SAR image characteristics. It also provides a useful feature extraction capability and an automatic quality assessment function. Our MrSARP model was tested on a standard dataset and showed significant improvements over state-of-the-art techniques in several aspects. Specifically, it enhanced the overall super-resolved image quality by 8.74 dB according to the SSIM index, preserved 91.18% of the inherent SAR image characteristics in the frequency domain, and boosted the network's generalization capability by 54.31%. Additionally, our MrSARP model achieved a notable 88.56% correlation between the assessed and actual QAs, indicating a very strong predictive capability. It is worth noting that the 88.56% correlation was significantly higher than the 76.81% achieved by the state-of-the-art model. Our MrSARP model has demonstrated superior performance, vast applications, and is ready for use in real-world scenarios. It has potential to be applied in areas such as agricultural monitoring, urban planning, and navigation systems. However, challenging conditions such as abnormal spine form, overlapping ribs, and limited field of view, make this task difficult. To address this issue, an algorithm using vertebral localization and identification has been developed to optimize extraction results. The algorithm adjusts the fitted model by moving each vertex along optimized paths that are based on projected and rotated versions of the ground truth. A novel technique uses a converged model to extract center coordinates, which then informs the optimization process. An efficient method calculates vertex displacement by multiplying small rotation matrices, allowing for rapid re-evaluation of the fitted model. By iterating this process, the algorithm iteratively improves its results. Evaluation against human annotations showed excellent results, with centroid errors of 1.46 and 1.65 mm for axial and sagittal orientations, respectively. The algorithm achieved a center error of 1.41 mm when evaluating sagittal and axial orientations simultaneously. Notably, the algorithm achieved nearly perfect vertebral center localization, with a dice score of 0.952 and 0.951 for sagittal and axial orientations. The developed algorithm successfully identified and localized vertebral centers in CT scans with an overall accuracy of 94.95%. Currents in random systems can be quantified using the Sant\'{e} and Leibler free-energy current vector and averaged locally in space. This paper establishes a connection between these currents and the widely used Widom distribution and outlines a method for determining equilibrium averages that are insensitive to the choice of current configuration. Additionally, the method allows for the extraction of gauge-invariant asymptotic data from numerical simulations. This is demonstrated in a one-dimensional system with competing interactions between adjacent sites. The resulting data is compared with existing results from other methods, revealing agreement within numerical precision. Further applications of this method to other models and systems are explored in the accompanying companion paper. In part II of this series, we discuss the practical implementation of this approach in numerical simulations. This involves introducing a framework that uses a Markov process basis to analyze and extract information from data obtained from multiple steady states. This Markov process basis allows for the efficient analysis of data from a wide range of systems, including those with long-range interactions and those that are three-dimensionally coupled. It is demonstrated that this method can be used to achieve a high level of precision in the extracted data. This is shown through a comparison of the extracted currents with those obtained from other, more traditional methods. In particular, we find that the precision of the Widom distribution's linear fit is improved by at least an order of magnitude in the regime where the system's flux is low. This method is found to be particularly suitable for systems that are thermodynamically coupled and those with a slow relaxation time. Further developments of this technique and its application to study the dynamics of other complex systems are proposed. This involves the use of this approach to identify the existence of additional steady states in open systems that are not detectable in equilibrium. This possibility is explored in the companion paper. In part III of this series, we discuss the generation of driving forces that are spatially non-uniform in a system with competing interactions. This is found to give rise to a variety of flow patterns that are observed to be stable over a wide range of driving forces. This is demonstrated through a combination of numerical simulation and theoretical analysis of the system's dynamics. This reveals that the existence of these stable flows can be identified by examining the Widom distribution's curvature, a property that can be determined from data obtained from numerical simulations. This finding opens up new possibilities for the use of the Sant\'{e} and Leibler free-energy current vector in the analysis of real-world fluids that are subject to non-uniform driving

Our data show that when we apply light to one crystal, the response is remarkable, with nearly 100% of the energy transferred to the second crystal at both optical and acoustic frequencies. Our findings also highlight the importance of light in facilitating energy transfer between coupled objects, a concept with far-reaching applications in advanced materials and devices. Additionally, we generate extensive data on the coupled oscillations in the systems, revealing the presence of multiple stable and metastable energy storage states. We introduce a novel optical storage system, grounded in the concept of reservoir physics, which utilizes aggregates of exciton-polaritons as the reservoir for information. The method leverages the unique characteristics of exciton-polaritons, enabling rapid and non-linear interactions between them. The storage capacity of this system is comprised of two elements: the optical trapping of polaritons and the system's recurrent grating formation ability. The first component enables the condensation of polaritons within a specific area through optical induction, serving as a mechanism that amplifies weak optical signals. The second component, stemming from the system's beam-coherent polariton lasing, allows the transfer of the trapped polaritons' phase information to the surrounding reservoir. We have developed a detailed theoretical framework to describe the system's behavior and have introduced two types of waveguide-based experiments for observing the artificial reservoir and transferring information within it. The outcomes of these experiments have pinpointed the system's confinement times, lasting from several microseconds to milliseconds, and have successfully demonstrated the transfer of information at a rate of 625 megabits per second. The developed concept has the capability to support faster information transfer rates in future developments. The presented work paves the road for integrating reservoir computing and exciton-polariton optics to develop groundbreaking optical information processing technologies. Additionally, we have established a distinct category of reservoir computers, characterized by unprecedented low propagation delays, which we refer to as the "zero-field regime" and believe it to be uniquely rich with numerous hidden patterns that require further in-depth analysis. It is hypothesized that the inherent nature of the polariton system could lead to an information flow pattern that is akin to that observed in biological brains and may offer novel insights into the underlying mechanics of this phenomenon. Therefore, this study not only discusses the technical particulars but also explores the underlying scientific concepts of this innovative approach to optical computing. In summary, we have developed a pioneering optical storage system, capable of transferring information at a rate of 625 megabits per second, and has introduced a novel category of reservoir computers, which may hold the key to understanding the fundamental nature of computing, particularly in relation to biological information processing. The unique characteristics of the system, such as its ability to enter a state of low propagation delay and potentially mimic biological information processing, make it an attractive solution for future reservoir-based computing applications. Furthermore, we have initiated two distinct approaches to optical computing, grounded in the concepts of exciton-polariton optics and zero-field regime, which could lead to breakthroughs

My fellow historian, Clifford Truesdell, once cautioned that historians should avoid attributing modern methods and attitudes to historical figures, whom he encouraged to speak in their own voice. I've tried to emulate this approach by giving Galileo a voice from the past, expressing his thoughts on mathematics and philosophy in a manner relevant to the scientific revolution. This 'voice' emerges from a reading of Galileo's writings, particularly those on philosophy, through the lens of Ignorantism - a philosophical movement that I believe influenced him. Ignorantism, characterized by a skeptical approach to certain knowledge and absolute truths, resembles a form of skepticism. This skeptical approach is not the same as nihilism, which would lead to a lack of knowledge. Rather, Skepticism and Ignorantism present a methodological tool for questioning established certainties and exploring possible knowledge. Galileo's philosophy, particularly in his later years when he was no longer a young man, is deeply rooted in Ignorantism. This interpretation offers a fresh perspective on Galileo's scientific methods and his approach to absolute truths, which he later discovered through his own observations. This discovery is not a consequence of his methods, which were actually quite traditional, but rather, it stems from the alignment of his methods with the principles of Ignorantism. This alignment enabled him to revise his initial understanding of the universe, which was based on traditional knowledge. Similarly, Newton's calculus, which he developed in conjunction with Leibniz, can be seen as an expression of the principles of Ignorantism. This interpretation is not a tribute to Clifford Truesdell's memory, but rather an acknowledgment of his wisdom in advising historians to speak in the voices of their subjects, rather than their own. By adopting this approach, historians can avoid projecting their own attitudes and ideas onto historical figures, whose actions and motivations may have been driven by entirely different forces. Galileo's story is a testament to the power of speaking in one's own voice, which led him to discover new possibilities and meanings, not only in his own life, but also in the scientific revolution as a whole. Finally, this interpretation is not an expression of my own views, but rather a demonstration of the virtues of counterfactual history, which I hope to elaborate upon in a future work. To study magnetic island coherence and merging behavior in turbulent and unstable plasma environments, we utilize the M3D-AMDT model, which integrates magnetohydrodynamics with embedded particle-in-cell simulations. This comprehensive approach enables us to investigate how magnetic surfaces interact and evolve within these chaotic plasma conditions. Beginning with a basic magnetohydrodynamic model that effectively captures the primary dynamics of coherent magnetic structures over extended periods of time, we can also employ a fully embedded particle-in-cell model for in-depth examination of specific processes. Our results reveal that magnetic island coherence and merging behavior can be effectively predicted based on the general magnetic flux conservation principle, and we observe a significant correlation between the embedded particle-in-cell simulations and the embedded test particle simulations in terms of merging rates and times. Additionally, as turbulence levels increase, we find a substantial decline in magnetic island coherence and merging rates. Notably, even at extremely low turbulence levels, we observe an isolated, highly coherent magnetic structure persisting for an extended period of time. This study provides an in-depth understanding of magnetic island coherence and merging behavior under diverse turbulent and unstable plasma conditions. Lastly, we identify a potential pathway for plasma energy release, and we propose integrating the M3D-AMDT model with other available tools to obtain a more comprehensive picture of this process. By combining the strengths of existing models, such as the NEMD model for nanosecond timescales and the M3D-AMDT model for microsecond timescales, we can achieve a comprehensive understanding of the entire process. Furthermore, we envision the integrated model having far-reaching applications in various fields, including laboratory experiments, stars, and planetary bodies. Emerging from our study is the concept that magnetic energy could be a significant driving force behind these phenomena. In particular, we find that the embedded particle-in-cell tests for the M3D-AMDT models demonstrate an impressive level of consistency with the general magnetic flux conservation principle, and we identify a significant merging barrier in the range of cm-lm intervals. This leads to a major discovery that the embedded particle-in-cell tests for the M3D-AMDT models may not be necessary for predicting merging rates and times, and we provide a simplified approach for estimating these metrics based on the general magnetic flux conservation principle. We present a novel technique in program analysis by investigating the relation between code comments and the developer who wrote them, particularly leveraging the comments' linguistic characteristics. This study introduces Scribe, an analytical tool designed to model a programmer's skill level based on expression usage in their comments. Using a vast dataset of Java projects from OpenSource, Scribe's training data, the research reveals that: (1) Scribe accurately classifies authors' skill levels; (2) Scribe's predictive accuracy remains consistent across various model configurations even with random training; (3) only 4 out of 19 linguistic features significantly impact prediction accuracy; (4) author groups sharing similar skill levels are overwhelmingly dominant; (5) comparing comments between programmers at different skill levels shows distinct differences in the features used. The findings illustrate the feasibility of analyzing programmers, an area of study within human-computer interaction known as understanding programmers. The research has the potential to contribute to extensive applications in empirical software studies, including detecting and preventing cheating on online learning platforms by identifying and training fake accounts. An open-source implementation of Scribe, as well as the associated data used in the study, are available on GitHub. The source code of Scribe, along with the related data, can be found at https://github.com/fasee/Scribe. The used data can be accessed at https://github.com/empirical-software-engineering/projects/tree/main/scribe-data. Scribe is based on CommentMiner, an analysis framework for Java code comments, also available on GitHub at https://github.com/fasee/CommentMiner. The current version of Scribe has been designed to analyze Java projects, but its concepts can be extended to other programming languages as well.
